#10556. Best Static Website Hosting Providers in 2027: Free and Paid Options Compared

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

You've finished building your website. The HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files are ready, everything works locally, and now you need somewhere to publish it.

Static website hosting is one of the simplest ways to get a website online. Many providers offer free plans, and you don't need to maintain a traditional web server.

The harder part is choosing the right provider. Some let you upload a single HTML file and share it immediately. Others connect to GitHub, automatically deploy code changes, and support entire development teams.

We've compared eight static hosting providers, including TiinyHost, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel, and GitHub Pages. Below, you'll find their free hosting limits, pricing, advantages, and drawbacks, along with recommendations for different types of projects.

Static website hosting is a service that stores and delivers pre-built website files, including HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and fonts.

Unlike traditional server-rendered websites, static sites don't need a server to generate each page when someone visits. The HTML is already prepared and can be delivered directly to the visitor's browser.

That doesn't mean static websites can't be interactive. JavaScript can still handle navigation, forms, filtering, and other features. Static sites can also communicate with external APIs or databases.

The main distinction is how pages are generated.

You can write a static website using plain HTML or generate one with frameworks and tools such as Astro, Hugo, Eleventy, or Next.js static export.

Static hosting is also commonly associated with Jamstack, an approach that separates the front end from back-end services.

Lower hosting costs: Many providers let you publish smaller websites for free.

Simpler maintenance: There's no application server or server-side runtime to maintain for the static pages themselves.

Efficient content delivery: Static files can be cached across a content delivery network (CDN), reducing the distance between visitors and website assets.

There are limitations, too. If your website requires user authentication, database operations, or server-side functionality, you'll need additional services or a hosting platform that supports them.

We compared eight providers based on their deployment methods, free plan allowances, pricing, and suitability for different projects.

Free hosting limits: Bandwidth, storage, build allowances, and restrictions.

Deployment process: Whether you can upload files directly or need a Git repository.

Custom domains and HTTPS: Support for publishing under your own domain.

Development features: Automatic deployments, preview environments, and integrations.

Pricing: What happens when a project exceeds its free allowance.

Usage restrictions: Whether free hosting is suitable for commercial projects.

The following table summarizes the main differences between all eight services.

Free plans aren't directly comparable. For example, Vercel restricts its Hobby plan to personal, non-commercial use, while GitHub Pages prohibits using the service as free hosting for an online business or commercial SaaS.

Bandwidth limits also aren't the same as visitor limits. A website serving large images or downloadable files can consume its monthly allowance with relatively few visitors.

Cloudflare Pages is a strong choice for developers who want to host static websites without worrying about a conventional monthly bandwidth cap.

You can connect a GitHub or GitLab repository, and Cloudflare automatically builds and deploys the website when you push changes. Direct uploads are also supported.

A maximum individual file size of 25 MiB.

The combination is useful for blogs, documentation websites, and other projects that primarily serve HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images.

Cloudflare also provides preview deployments, custom domains, and HTTPS support.

No fixed bandwidth cap for static asset delivery.

Generous free plan for typical static websites.

Monthly build limits can matter for frequently updated projects.

Cloudflare's product range can make the initial setup less straightforward for beginners.

Cloudflare is increasingly emphasizing Workers Static Assets for new projects. Pages remains available, but developers starting a new application should compare both deployment approaches.

For a conventional static website, however, Pages is still a practical option, particularly when traffic could grow beyond the limits of other free plans.

See the official Cloudflare Pages limits for the current allowances.

Netlify combines static website hosting with tools designed to make development and deployment easier.

Connect a Git repository, configure your build settings, and Netlify can publish a new version whenever you push changes.

It also creates deploy previews, allowing you to inspect changes before merging them into your production branch.

This is useful when multiple people work on the same website or when you want to review design changes before publishing.

Netlify supports custom domains, HTTPS, serverless functions, and form handling.

Netlify's free plan uses a credit-based model with 300 credits per month.

Production deployments consume 15 credits each.

Web requests consume 2 credits per 10,000 requests.

Deploy previews and branch deployments consume no deployment credits.

The paid Personal plan starts at $9 per month and includes 1,000 monthly credits.

Convenient Git integration and deploy previews.

Built-in features such as forms and serverless functions.

Suitable for both simple websites and more advanced front-end projects.

Credit-based pricing requires monitoring several types of usage.

A busy site with frequent deployments can consume its free allowance faster than expected.

When comparing Netlify alternatives, Cloudflare Pages is particularly worth considering if your main concern is bandwidth.

For developers choosing between Vercel vs Netlify, the deciding factor is often the framework and workflow. Netlify offers a flexible approach to static site deployment, while Vercel has particularly close integration with Next.js.

Vercel is particularly well suited to Next.js applications, although it also supports React, Vue, Svelte, Astro, and other frameworks.

Like Netlify, Vercel connects to your Git repository and deploys updates automatically.

Every deployment receives its own URL, which helps developers review changes before publishing them to the main website.

Vercel also supports server-side rendering, functions, and other features beyond traditional static site hosting.

There is one important restriction: Vercel Hobby is intended for personal, non-commercial use only.

If you're deploying a business website or another commercial project, you'll need an appropriate paid plan.

Convenient deployment workflow for Next.js.

Supports both static and server-rendered applications.

Paid usage can involve multiple resource-based charges.

If you're building a personal Next.js application, Vercel is an obvious candidate. For a basic HTML website, however, its additional framework features may be unnecessary.

GitHub Pages is a straightforward way to publish a website directly from a GitHub repository.

It works particularly well for developer portfolios, project documentation, open-source websites, and small informational sites.

You can upload HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files to a repository, configure GitHub Pages, and publish them under a github.io subdomain.

GitHub Pages can serve existing static files or build websites using supported workflows, including Jekyll and GitHub Actions.

Published websites have a maximum size of 1 GB.

Bandwidth has a soft limit of 100 GB per month.

Free accounts can publish Pages sites from public repositories.

The bandwidth and build restrictions are soft limits, meaning they aren't necessarily enforced as strict cutoffs.

Simple integration with GitHub repositories.

Well suited to documentation and open-source projects.

Free accounts require a public repository for Pages.

GitHub Pages is not intended for running online businesses, e-commerce websites, or commercial SaaS products.

GitHub Pages is particularly convenient if your code already lives on GitHub and you only need to publish documentation or a portfolio.

For commercial websites, Cloudflare Pages or Netlify may be more appropriate.

The GitHub Pages documentation explains its hosting limits and usage restrictions.

Not every website needs a repository, deployment pipeline, or command-line interface.

If you've created a simple HTML page and want to share it, TiinyHost lets you upload an HTML file or ZIP archive and publish it under a shareable URL.

It can also host PDFs, making it useful for sharing documents and presentations alongside website projects.

The main advantage is the upload process. You don't need to configure a repository or install development tools before publishing.

Sharing an HTML file with someone who doesn't use Git.

The free plan includes one active site, a 3 MB project upload limit, and an allowance of 5,000 monthly visits.

The Tiny plan costs €5 per month when billed monthly. It supports uploads up to 25 MB and includes built-in analytics.

The Solo plan starts at €13 per month when billed monthly and adds features such as custom domains, password protection, and additional projects.

Annual billing is available at lower effective monthly prices.

No Git repository or command line required.

Suitable for previews and smaller projects.

The free plan's 3 MB limit is restrictive for websites with many images or other assets.

Custom domains require the Solo plan or higher.

Upload-based publishing is less convenient than Git automation for frequently updated websites.

For someone who simply needs free HTML hosting to share a small project, TiinyHost is worth considering.

For a larger production website that receives regular updates, Git-based hosting is likely to be more manageable.

Firebase Hosting is Google's hosting service for static websites and web application assets.

It integrates with other Firebase products, including Authentication, Cloud Firestore, and Cloud Functions.

That makes it useful when a website needs static hosting but also relies on Google's back-end services.

Deployment is handled through the Firebase command-line interface.

After configuring your project, you can deploy using:

Firebase distributes website assets through its CDN and supports custom domains with SSL certificates.

The Blaze plan uses pay-as-you-go billing while retaining applicable no-cost allowances.

One detail worth checking is the distinction between Firebase Hosting and Firebase App Hosting. They are separate products with different features and pricing models.

Integrates with Firebase Authentication and Firestore.

Useful for applications already using Google's developer services.

Initial setup is more involved than uploading an HTML file.

The daily transfer allowance may become restrictive for larger websites.

Firebase Hosting makes the most sense when Firebase is already part of your application.

For a standalone static blog or portfolio that doesn't use Firebase services, Cloudflare Pages or GitHub Pages may be simpler.

Amazon S3 and CloudFront offer a different approach to static hosting.

Instead of using a platform that handles the entire deployment process, you combine AWS services to store and deliver your website.

S3 stores the website files, while CloudFront distributes them through a CDN.

This setup provides control over caching, permissions, security, and integration with other AWS services.

It can be suitable for organizations already using AWS or developers who need specific infrastructure configurations.

AWS uses usage-based pricing for S3 storage, requests, and applicable CloudFront usage.

Free allowances may apply depending on your account and the current AWS pricing program, but you should calculate costs based on your expected traffic, storage, and requests.

Unlike simpler hosting services, there isn't one fixed monthly price for every website.

Several services can contribute to the final bill.

Incorrect permissions or origin settings can cause access errors.

One common issue when setting up S3 static website hosting is receiving a 403 Forbidden error because of bucket permissions or CloudFront origin configuration.

AWS recommends using CloudFront Origin Access Control with a regular S3 bucket origin so that the bucket can remain private. This differs from exposing the S3 website endpoint directly, which does not support HTTPS on its own.

AWS S3 and CloudFront are worth considering if you need that level of control. For a small static website, a managed hosting platform usually requires less setup.

Render is a cloud platform that supports static websites alongside web services, databases, background workers, and other application components.

Its static hosting works through a Git repository.

Connect your repository, select the build command and publish directory, and Render automatically deploys your website.

The service includes CDN delivery, custom domains, and managed TLS certificates.

Render is particularly useful when your project includes both a static front end and back-end services that you want to manage through the same platform.

Render's Hobby workspace is free and includes:

500 standard build pipeline minutes per month.

Additional bandwidth is billed at $0.15 per GB under the current pricing structure, so the Hobby workspace should not be treated as unlimited free hosting.

The Pro workspace costs $25 per month, excluding any applicable usage-based compute charges.

Static websites and back-end services on one platform.

The 5 GB included bandwidth allowance is relatively small.

Render makes sense when you're already using it for other parts of an application.

If you only need to host a static HTML website, Cloudflare Pages offers a more generous bandwidth allowance without the additional platform complexity.

Free static website hosting can be sufficient for a personal portfolio, documentation site, prototype, or small informational website.

However, the restrictions vary considerably between providers.

Some hosts measure data transfer, while others use visitor counts or a credit system. Check how each provider calculates usage rather than comparing headline numbers alone.

If your website rebuilds whenever you publish content, deployment limits matter. A blog updated a few times a month has different requirements from an application receiving dozens of deployments every day.

Free hosting doesn't always mean you can run a business website. Vercel's Hobby plan and GitHub Pages have restrictions that may rule out certain commercial projects.

Some services include custom domains on free plans. Others require an upgrade before you can connect one.

A free plan might stop serving additional usage, while another provider may bill for overages.

Before publishing a production website, check the provider's billing behavior and configure spending controls where available.

The right service depends primarily on how you build your website and what you intend to do with it.

For most developers publishing a conventional static website, Cloudflare Pages is a reasonable starting point.

If you're working with Git and want convenient previews and deployment tools, Netlify is another good choice.

For small files, temporary demos, and client previews, a simpler upload-based service may save time.

You should also consider how often the website will change.

Uploading files manually may be fine for a page that rarely changes. For a website with regular content updates, automated deployments from Git will generally be easier to maintain.

Publishing your website is only the first step. If you want search engines to discover and understand your pages, check the technical SEO basics before sharing the URL.

Every important page should have a descriptive HTML title and a relevant meta description.

You can use the Meta Tags Generator to create the necessary markup.

Open Graph tags help control how a page appears when shared on platforms that support them.

Set the title, description, canonical page URL where appropriate, and preview image.

A robots.txt file tells compliant crawlers which paths they may access. It doesn't guarantee indexing or prevent a public page from appearing in search results.

Use the Robots.txt Generator to create your crawler rules.

Include a sitemap with the canonical URLs you want search engines to discover.

Structured data helps search engines interpret eligible content.

Depending on the website, you may want Organization, Article, BreadcrumbList, or other relevant schema types.

The JSON-LD Schema Generator can help generate markup.

Confirm the correct domain loads over HTTPS.

Check canonical tags and redirect behavior.

Make sure important pages don't contain unintended noindex directives.

Test page performance and Core Web Vitals.

Verify the website in Google Search Console.

Static hosting makes serving website files relatively straightforward, but technical SEO still requires configuration and testing.

Cloudflare Pages is a good general-purpose choice because of its free static asset bandwidth and Git integration. Netlify is well suited to teams that need deploy previews, while GitHub Pages works well for portfolios and documentation. The best option depends on your deployment workflow, traffic requirements, and whether the website is commercial.

Yes. TiinyHost, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, GitHub Pages, Firebase Hosting, Render, and several other services offer free hosting options. Most free plans have restrictions involving bandwidth, deployments, storage, or usage. Check the terms before using a free plan for a business website.

A small static website can cost nothing to host if it stays within a provider's free allowances. Paid plans vary from fixed monthly subscriptions to usage-based pricing. Domain registration, paid back-end services, and additional storage or bandwidth may increase the total cost.

For a standalone HTML file, upload-based hosting is generally the simplest approach. Services such as TiinyHost let you publish a file without configuring Git or a build process. If the project already lives in a GitHub repository, GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages may be more convenient.

GitHub Pages is a sensible option for documentation, open-source projects, and personal portfolios. Netlify offers more deployment features, including preview environments, forms, and functions. It also supports commercial projects, making it more appropriate for some business websites that would fall outside GitHub Pages' permitted uses.

Static website hosting doesn't need to be expensive or complicated. The important part is choosing a service that matches your website and deployment process.

Cloudflare Pages is a good starting point for static websites that need generous free bandwidth. Netlify is useful for Git-based development, while GitHub Pages suits personal projects and documentation.

If you're publishing a small HTML file or sharing a prototype, upload-based hosting may be all you need.

#10555. How the effects of Jensen Huang’s ouster are spiraling out through the economy

Nvidia and Jensen Huang aren’t the only ones in the crosshairs. 

The longtime tech executive has had a bad week. It all began when news surfaced that Huang had been having an extramarital affair with an alleged spy for the Chinese government. In response, the corporate board of Nvidia—the company Huang cofounded more than 30 years ago—began an investigation. The FBI launched a probe, too. Then news broke Wednesday that Huang had engaged in at least one other affair, this time with a company executive who reported directly to him.

By Thursday morning, Huang had resigned, and the chip company had appointed an interim CEO. But the hits kept coming. Thursday afternoon Reuters reported that Huang had engaged in an affair with a second employee.

Obviously, this is bad news for Nvidia. Stocks are down, and Democrats, now preparing to take back Congress, appear to be ramping up plans to investigate the company and any possible risks to U.S. national security. But this is also bad for a range of other entities that have a stake in Nvidia’s success.

Here are a few that stand to feel some of the blowback. 

The White House

The White House, fresh off of devastating losses in the midterm elections, stands to face questions about why it held off on taking action after it learned about Huang’s affair with an alleged spy. The Trump administration already had a poor reputation for security and intelligence practices, but seemingly sleeping on this knowledge is all but certain to raise the prospect of further probes. 

Trump officials, notably, have cleared deals allowing Nvidia to sell advanced computer chips to China, and even leveraged U.S. influence over the company’s chips in geopolitical negotiations. 

Current and prospective NVIDIA customers

The U.S. AI supply chain runs on Nvidia. OpenAI, Anthropic, and a slew of other large language model developers rely on the company’s hardware. Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle are also major customers. This is, in large part, because GPUs—or graphics processing units—are particularly adept at the kinds of computations needed to develop large reasoning models. 

Now, with so much scrutiny on Nvidia, there’s a risk those companies—and any deals in progress—might face headwinds as the still-scrambling board figures out what to do next. The Semiconductor Industry Association, a major trade group that advocates for chip companies, declined to comment. Hugging Face, an AI developer that agreed to an acquisition by Nvidia earlier this year, did not respond to a request for comment. 

Remarkably, Huang doesn’t seem to have had a succession plan. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was appointed interim CEO on Thursday morning. 

The scandal and disarray isn’t just bad for American companies that need Nvidia’s chips. Given the extent to which Huang advocated for loosening chip sale limits to China, any customers with suspected links to the Chinese government may also see far more scrutiny on Nvidia deals than before. 

U.S. federal agencies

The U.S. government is a major supporter of Nvidia, using the company’s tech extensively in its own systems, including classified networks. The revelations this week are not only embarrassing for the government, but raise concerns about the extent to which government officials were aware of Huang’s affair with a suspected spy for China, and how they might have influenced the company’s dealings with federal agencies.

One former federal chief information officer told Fast Company that the scandal raises suspicions that the U.S. security clearance system, which is supposed to engage in continuous monitoring, isn’t as up to snuff as it should be. 

Everyone else 

We really are that dependent on Nvidia. If we learned anything from the chip shortage we experienced during the pandemic, the semiconductor market is heavily concentrated, and disruptions with just one company can quickly ripple through the economy. In 2020, it was companies like TSMC, a Taiwan-based contract manufacturer that supplies chips for a host of devices. And the stock market—including pension funds and 401(k) plans—are deeply exposed to Nvidia stock.

“It is striking that Nvidia, a $4 trillion company central to both the AI economy and U.S. equity markets, appears to have no publicly identified successor to Jensen Huang,” Ann Lewis, a technology executive and former U.S. government tech official, told Fast Company Wednesday. “In cybersecurity, we call this a single point of failure. A company of this scale should not depend so completely on one person’s relationships and judgment.”

#10552. Trump’s suggestion for the next Nvidia CEO is another tech titan he’s already close with

With Jensen Huang officially out as president and CEO of Nvidia, rumors are swirling over who will take his place at the helm of one of the world’s biggest tech companies. Could it be interim CEO Colette Kress, who’s spent more than a decade as Nvidia’s executive vice president and CFO? Or maybe company cofounder Chris Malachowsky, now a senior vice president of engineering and operations?

President Donald Trump has his own idea. His left-field pick: former Apple CEO Tim Cook. In a post on Truth Social, Trump announced his preference for Huang’s successor.

“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump wrote. “A Legend replaces a Legend!”

Beyond Trump’s dubious claim that Huang did “a fantastic job” as CEO—having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy might disqualify him from that distinction—Cook is far from an obvious pick to step into the role.

Cook only recently transitioned out of his CEO role at Apple, becoming the company’s executive chairman in September. In a meeting announcing the decision, Cook spelled out the considerations that allowed for the shift: The “business had to be doing great,” the “product road map [had] to be incredible,” and his replacement, former senior vice president of hardware engineering John Ternus, had to be “ready for the role.” With all those conditions met, “now was the time,” Cook said.

Why, then, would Trump want Cook to take on another CEO mantle? Notably, the two have gotten close during Trump’s second term as president.

Trump and Cook, sitting in a tree

Trump and Cook weren’t always buddies. During Trump’s first term, he infamously referred to Cook as “Tim Apple,” seemingly forgetting his name.

But since Trump took back the office in 2025, Cook has frequently been spotted at the president’s side, from attending a White House dinner for tech CEOs last September to watching an early screening of first lady Melania Trump’s documentary in early 2026.

For his part, Cook insists he’s not politically aligned with Trump, instead abstaining from politics entirely.

“What I do is I interact on policy, not politics. I’m not a political person on either side. I’m not political,” Cook said in an interview with Good Morning America earlier this year. “I’m kind of straight down the middle. And I focus on policy, so I’m very pleased that the president and the administration is accessible to talk about policy.”

That purported focus on policy aligns with Cook’s intentions for his role as Apple’s executive chairman, which include overseeing the company’s global relations. “This is an area where we’ve built relationships over multiple years . . . and I think I can help with that,” Cook said when announcing his step-down.

#10551. Meta’s Horizon+ looks to become Meta VR+ and include 3D movies

Meta Horizon+ is rumored to be changing its name to Meta VR+ and may start including movies in addition to games with the subscription price.

Meta’s quest (ahem) to distance itself from the Horizon era is in full swing, and the latest rumor says it’s time for the company’s Game Pass-like subscription to change its brand name. VR leaker Nori posted a screenshot on X showing a handful of 3D movies coming to the Meta VR Plus service. Considering there is no such Meta VR Plus service currently, the obvious conclusion is that Meta Horizon+ is being renamed once again.

Meta Horizon+ currently includes over 100 games with its $7.99 per month subscription and is similar to Microsoft’s Xbox Game Pass service in many ways. Unironically, Meta Horizon+ also includes the basic Xbox Game Pass tier with over 50 Xbox games playable via the Game Pass cloud. Meta offers a 3-month trial with every new Meta Quest purchase.

The new Meta VR+ service is purported to include 3D movies as well, although we don’t yet know if this will be included in the regular $7.99 per month rate, or if Meta will be introducing additional content tiers, as services like Netflix, Disney+, Xbox Game Pass, and others do. Based on the screenshot, these will be big-name movies and are likely positioned to enhance the value of the upcoming $1,300 Meta VR Glasses, although all the same content will work on existing Meta Quest 3 units.

Meta has been slowly distancing itself from the “Horizon” name ever since the beginning of this year, when its VR division got a big reset. In a February blog post, Samantha Ryan, the VP of Content at Meta’s Reality Labs, spoke about the changes to the company’s strategy, including the loss of most in-house VR gaming studios. Since then, several prominent VR developers from Meta have gone on to create independent studios, including the super-popular Supernatural exercise app.

Meta then decoupled the unpopular Horizon Metaverse from its headsets, moving it to mobile-only, and has been removing the “Horizon” name from just about everything since then. Meta Horizon+ looks to be the latest big change, as the company moves toward “Meta VR” branding, which is clearer and separates its VR division from mobile and smart glasses efforts.

Microsoft, the tech giant that is building 35 data centers around the U.S. and has plans for 134 more, has reportedly met with the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and the National Security Council as the FCC is considering an import ban on Chinese optical transceivers. According to Reuters, the company, alongside the Information Technology Industry Council (ITI), is lobbying against the move.

“It really threatens to arguably grind (the data center rollout) to a halt,” ITI Executive Vice President of Policy and General Counsel John Miller said. He also added, “Those chips, without optical transceivers, literally could just sit there waiting around unutilized until you actually have the transceivers to essentially connect them together,” referring to the AI chips that data centers use.

Optical transceivers are tiny modules plugged into hardware that convert their electrical signals into light signals, allowing data to be transmitted as light pulses across fiber optics. Data centers increasingly use optical transceivers and fiber optics to transmit data between AI GPUs and server racks, as they’re faster, offer lower latency, require less power, and generate less heat compared to traditional copper connections. However, Chinese companies currently supply 66% of the global market, meaning banning them from supplying data centers in the U.S. would more than halve the available supply, thereby exacerbating the various shortages that have been pummeling the industry.

However, there are concerns that some of these transceivers could be compromised by Beijing and be used to steal data, install malware, or remotely disrupt American data centers, which is why the FCC is considering the restriction, just like how it banned Huawei from the U.S. telecommunications network. But unlike Huawei, which had many established competitors in the telecommunications hardware industry, only two U.S.-based companies produce optical transceivers that data centers need — Coherent and Lumentum. While these firms could produce optical transceivers to compete with Chinese offerings, they simply do not have the scale to make up for the shortfall if the FCC bans Chinese imports today.

One compromise floated by the Trump administration is that it would only ban Chinese optical transceivers capable of hitting 3.2 terabits per second. While this technology already exists, its production isn’t expected to expand until 2028, with installation not beginning until 2029. This should give American producers time to ramp up their own output, although the suggestion is still under consideration.

#10547. A major change to the U.S. mortgage market could be coming. Here’s why homeowners should care

As President Donald Trump enters the lame-duck era of his presidency, questions remain about which of his various agenda items will actually get accomplished.

One of his long-standing goals has been to end the government conservatorship that mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have been subject to since the financial crisis of 2008. After failing to make much headway during his first term in office, Trump revived those intentions for his second term—but once again hasn’t made it much of a priority.

This past May, Trump posted on Truth Social that he was “working on taking these amazing companies public,” while adding that the U.S. government would retain its mortgage guarantees and oversight role for both government-sponsored entities. But only a matter of days later, when asked about an initial public offering for Fannie and Freddie, Trump said: “It’s not a rush.”

Meanwhile, Trump also sees the current government control of Fannie and Freddie as an opportunity to address housing affordability. On the eve of the midterm elections, he announced at a rally in Kansas that the entities would invest $4.3 billion in home loans in the state next year, which he promised would help 15,000 people achieve their American dream.

Removing Fannie and Freddie from conservatorship, experts have cautioned, could push up mortgage rates. And because Democrats regained control of Congress by campaigning on affordability, that may make them reluctant to entertain an end to this long-standing conservatorship now, when so many Americans are grappling with an affordability crisis. 

Further complicating matters is how, exactly, the Trump administration could go about ending the conservatorship—whether by an executive order or with support from Congress. Legal and political analysts are divided on whether that could happen or if Trump would need support from Congress, as Realtor.com reported.  

Frank Cassidy, the former federal housing commissioner in Trump’s second term, told the outlet that Trump can privatize Fannie and Freddie without Republican control of Congress, but noted that how they were structured post-conservatorship would matter. 

“It hasn’t been a priority yet,” Cassidy told Realtor.com. “It would need to be worked on very quickly because it will take some time.” 

A PUSH FROM WALL STREET

One person who’d very much like privatizing Fannie and Freddie to be a priority is hedge funder Bill Ackman. He says that removing these entities from conservatorship would be “helpful” for improving housing affordability because it would remove any political uncertainty from the mortgage market, particularly if Democrats were to use Fannie and Freddie in the future to “achieve political objectives.”

Of course, he has an incentive at stake: His firm, Pershing Square, is invested in both Fannie and Freddie. Though the companies were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010, they have traded in the over-the-counter market ever since.

Still, Ackman argues that Americans stand to benefit from ending the conservatorship. “This is a major point of economic policy where the president can have a hundreds of billion-dollar win for the American people,” he told CNBC, adding that it could be a “windfall” to the tune of $500 billion.

WEIGHING THE CONSEQUENCES

Such optimism for a widespread benefit to Americans counters what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expressed on a 2Way podcast appearance last month. 

While Bessent said that the Trump administration will tackle the ownership structure of Fannie and Freddie in either 2027 or 2028, he said the “north star” guiding a decision will be whether ending the conservatorship can be accomplished without meaningfully increasing the spread between mortgage-backed securities and Treasury yields.

“It’s unclear why homeowners or mortgage holders would benefit from a change in the arrangement of the shareholder structure,” Bessent said.

What people on both sides of the political aisle can agree on is that a rush to end an 18-year arrangement would be most problematic. Still, the clock is ticking on Trump’s time in office to accomplish this goal, with less than 800 days remaining. 

And one person who could stand in the way is Rep. Maxine Waters, a Democrat from California, who is running to chair the House Financial Services Committee again after serving on it for more than a decade. 

As Realtor.com reported, Waters has historically opposed any efforts to rapidly end the conservatorship without comprehensive congressional oversight. “To address the affordable housing crisis, Congress must ensure that Fannie and Freddie meet their mission to provide liquidity, sustainability, and affordability to all housing markets in the U.S., and at all times,” Waters said at a hearing in April.

Stingray systems are deployed in salmon pens along the Norwegian coast, protecting over 112 million fish.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Submarine AI laser robots have been a surefire success for Norwegian salmon farmers, according to the most recent annual report from the aptly named Stingray Marine Solutions. The Oslo, Norway-based firm now has over 3,500 units deployed around salmon pens along the Norwegian coast, protecting over 112 million fish. Stingray deployments are up by about 1,000 over the last year. This operation has grown to become one of the largest commercial AI deployments in Scandinavia.

These high-tech AI-enhanced submarines protect 20-25% of farmed salmon in the country, according to the latest figures. Using this high-tech AI laser solution to ‘optically delouse’ the salmon means fish don’t have to be passed through harsh chemical baths to prevent infestations of these tiny parasitic crustaceans. The result is improved salmon growth and welfare, and consistently cleaner fish exhibit reduced mortality.

The video above shows a behind-the-scenes peek at the 250-employee-strong Stingray operation. There’s some colorful laser action with two Stingrays seen zapping away in a salmon pen included in the clip. They use AI to recognize and target the sea lice.

Sea lice are a big problem for fish farmers, with the control of these parasites being a central challenge for the industry. Traditionally, measures such as chemical treatments were used to help control the buildup of sea lice. However, while chemicals can treat a large number of fish simultaneously, they can be bad for the environment, can stress fish, lice can develop resistance, and the introduction of any kind of poison or toxin into food production isn’t usually good for humans either.

In contrast, the Stingray AI laser system identifies and targets only sea lice, works continuously 24/7 as the fish go around normally in their pens, and avoids any chemical introduction or resistance issues. The reduction in sea lice around the farming area is better for other wild fish populations nearby, too.

Solutions like Stingray do have a few drawbacks. Primarily, fish farming businesses might look sheepishly at the up-front costs of deployment. Moreover, it might be best used as a preventative measure, keeping localized lice populations low. The Stingray’s range is limited now by its deployment in the salmon pens, so lice can gather in darker, murkier corners and outside their patrol area.

#10543. CEOs still think they can get away with affairs after #MeToo

Nearly a decade after the #MeToo movement burst into public consciousness, the upheaval at Nvidia may be a lesson in how little CEOs seem to have learned. 

Nvidia’s embattled CEO, Jensen Huang, has resigned following a New York Times report on Wednesday that revealed he had engaged in another extramarital relationship—this time involving a subordinate, the company’s vice president of healthcare and one of his 60 direct reports. The affair was a blatant violation of Nvidia’s code of conduct, which notes that employees should steer clear of situations that could create a conflict of interest, including “personal relationships.” The company also purports to “promptly investigate” reports of misconduct.

While this dalliance has fewer national security implications than his entanglement with an alleged Chinese spy, it does suggest that CEOs like Huang don’t expect to face consequences for getting involved with employees. 

Huang is in good company: Many employers have similar policies that forbid romantic relationships between managers and their direct reports, but that hasn’t stopped executives from crossing the line anyway. (Who could forget the viral video of the Astronomer CEO caught canoodling with his chief people officer at a Coldplay concert?)

In recent years, however, a number of executives have been forced to step down after pursuing inappropriate relationships, in addition to CEOs like Leslie Moonves (formerly head of CBS) being fired for sexual harassment. 

Back in 2019, McDonald’s then-CEO Steve Easterbrook was ousted over a relationship with a subordinate. Later he was sued by the company for concealing other relationships with employees and misleading investors. (He was eventually forced to pay back his $105 million severance package.)

There was Alan Shaw, former CEO of Norfolk Southern railroad, who was let go in 2024 over his relationship with the company’s chief legal officer. Last year, Nestlé SA CEO Laurent Freixe was given the boot after an internal investigation confirmed a relationship with a subordinate (which Freixe had initially denied). Kohl’s CEO Ashley Buchanan was also recently forced out when the board learned that he had given millions of dollars in business to a vendor he was dating without disclosing the relationship.

The fact that CEOs continue to pursue their subordinates, regardless of the consequences, may seem like a sign that the #MeToo movement is in the rearview. Perhaps some executives truly believe they are irreplaceable, or that there is now limited public pressure, years after #MeToo took hold. 

But Amy Nicole Baker, a professor at the University of New Haven who studies workplace romance, argues that not much has shifted after #MeToo, either in terms of CEO behavior or how companies tend to handle these situations. 

“The stock price goes down, at least in the short term,” she says, citing her research on how stock prices are impacted by sexual harassment allegations or affairs involving the CEO. “And usually CEOs are removed and replaced.”

Boards tend to have limited tolerance for the behavior, which they view as a sign of poor judgment. Indiscretions like an extramarital affair or otherwise inappropriate relationship can set off alarm bells or lead board members to wonder what else a CEO is hiding. “Boards look at CEO behavior as a signal for what could be going on in the internal management of the company,” Baker says.  

Still, it appears CEOs don’t necessarily feel constrained by those expectations, or the rules they impose on their employees—even when their own peers have been in the line of fire. 

“People show less restraint when they are in power, and they’re also more likely to perceive someone else sending them sexual signals when they’re actually not,” Baker says. “So the research on power can tell us a little bit about why this keeps happening.” 

People in positions of power tend to be more impulsive and comfortable with risk—something they are often rewarded for in a business context. Company culture can also reinforce that behavior, if it’s more informal and encourages people to push boundaries. “If you’re willing to break a rule in one way, it’s probably more acceptable to tacitly break a rule in a different way,” Baker says. 

The intense scrutiny of Huang’s misdeeds might discourage some CEOs from engaging in relationships with subordinates or other inappropriate behavior—but likely not for long. 

“In terms of the CEOs and their propensity to get involved in risky workplace relationships, that doesn’t seem to have changed,” Baker says. “More people are willing to say, ‘Yes, this happened to me. Yes, this is an issue. Yes, this is a problem.’ There’s certainly more recognition and awareness. But when it comes to people at this highest echelon, I’m not seeing a change in behavior.”

People are already calling out sick to play the feverishly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI. Companies like Logitech are even giving staff paid time off to partake. 

Now, thanks to prediction market Kalshi, folks won’t have to play hooky from their jobs to dive into the video game—the first installment in 13 years of Rockstar Games’ hit franchise that has earned the company billions worldwide. Instead, one person can make playing it their literal job.

Kalshi will pay a lucky gamer between $100,000 and $120,000 to play Grand Theft Auto VI’s story mode through to completion, starting right at midnight on launch day, November 19. The winning applicant will stream their digital criminal adventures on YouTube or Twitch as they explore the fictional U.S. state of Leonida as the Bonnie-and-Clyde main character couple, Jason and Lucia.

The ideal candidate is “an experienced gamer” and “streamer with your own channel,” the listing states, along with “18+ years of life IRL, 10+ years of sweaty gaming, 3+ years of streaming experience.” They’ll get an extra $15,000 upon completion of the project.

As Kalshi’s “researcher”—and yes, per the LinkedIn post, the company assures that this is a real job—the winning candidate will be tasked with exploring and studying Leonida’s in-game economy of robberies and heists, perfecting the “optimal moneymaking strategy” and building “a spreadsheet to prove it,” to the point where they’ll get “accused of ruining the game for everyone else.”

In addition to unpacking the way fictional money moves in Vice City, the researcher is apparently also tasked with monitoring the game’s effects on the actual economy—tracking, for example, “who called in ‘sick,’ how DoorDash carried the entire nation through launch week, and how much productivity America lost,” the listing states. 

Kalshi’s interest in the cultural and economic impacts of the game are well founded: The Wall Street Journal has warned of a “work blackout” upon its release, and one Spanish economist estimated the U.S. economy will lose $1 billion in productivity due to absenteeism.

And according to a poll released last month that surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults 18 or older who are employed full time and play video games regularly, 39% said they were planning to request time off in advance to play GTA VI, 36% said they’ll call in sick, and 32% said they’d “work” from home on release day. Many anticipate catching “GTA flu.”

Grand Theft Auto VI, which is being called “the biggest entertainment launch in history,” arrives Thursday, November 19, on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S consoles. Digital preorders have broken records, generating $1 billion from over 10 million units sold worldwide, according to estimates.

The researcher listing hasn’t even been up for 24 hours, and “over 100 people have clicked apply,” according to the LinkedIn post—something nobody needed Kalshi to predict.

#10539. A Practical Introduction to the Twitch Helix API

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Behind almost every Twitch tool you have ever seen, the stat trackers, the moderation bots, the stream overlays, the alert systems, sits one interface: the Twitch Helix API. Twitch is unusually generous with public data, and Helix is the door to it. If you have ever wondered how third-party sites know who is live, what a channel's viewership looks like, or details a Twitch profile page does not even display, this is the machinery.

This article is a practical overview of Helix for developers who have not used it yet: what it offers, how its authentication works, what people build with it, and where the sharp edges are.

Helix is Twitch's current REST API, served from api.twitch.tv/helix. It replaced the old "Kraken" API, which was fully retired in 2022, so any tutorial still showing Kraken endpoints is a sign to keep scrolling. Helix covers users, streams, channels, games and categories, clips, chat, moderation actions, subscriptions, and events, with JSON in and JSON out.

Two things distinguish it from many platform APIs. First, a large share of it works without any user's permission, because the data is public by Twitch's own definition. Second, it is paired with EventSub, a push system that notifies your application when things happen (a stream goes live, a user follows, a message arrives) instead of forcing you to poll. Most serious Twitch tools use both: Helix for lookups, EventSub for live events.

Authentication is where most newcomers stall, mainly because Twitch offers several OAuth flows and tutorials rarely say which one you actually need. The short version:

Every request needs a Client ID, which you get by registering an application in the Twitch developer console (two-factor authentication on your account is required first). Requests carry the Client ID and a bearer token together; forgetting the Client ID header is the classic mystery 401.

App access tokens come from the client credentials flow, a single server-to-server request with your ID and secret. They have no user attached and that is fine, because public reads, user profiles, live streams, top games, clips, need no user context. For most read-only tools, this is the only flow you ever touch.

Tokens expire, so real applications cache them with their reported lifetime and refresh on a 401 rather than assuming a token lives forever.

A tour of the endpoints that power most tools:

Users. Give the users endpoint a username and it returns the account's public record: display name, profile image, description, Affiliate or Partner status, and the account's exact creation timestamp. That last field is interesting because Twitch does not display it anywhere on a profile, yet it is one of the platform's most useful trust signals, moderators use account age to spot throwaway accounts, and streamers use it to filter giveaway entries. The creation date alone powers a small subcategory of tools: free account age checkers, such as Twitch account age checker, are essentially this one endpoint with a clean page around it, taking any public username and returning the creation date, age, avatar, and broadcaster status. It is a good illustration of how far a single well-chosen Helix field can go.

Streams. The stream's endpoint reports who is live right now, with titles, categories, thumbnail URLs, and viewer counts. This is the backbone of every "is my favorite streamer live" notifier and every directory-style site, and polling it over time is how stat trackers chart viewership history.

Games and categories. Top games, category search, and metadata. Combined with streams data, this is how analytics sites rank categories and how tools answer "how crowded is this category right now."

Clips and videos. Clip metadata, view counts, and creation tools. Highlight compilers and clip-sharing bots live here.

Helix enforces a points-based rate limit per Client ID, and every response tells you where you stand through Ratelimit-Limit, Ratelimit-Remaining, and Ratelimit-Reset headers. Well-behaved tools read those headers and back off before hitting zero; badly behaved ones retry 429s in a loop and wonder why things get worse. For lookup-style tools the practical fix is caching, data like account creation dates never changes, so there is no reason to ask twice.

A few more edges worth knowing before they bite:

Usernames change, IDs do not. Store user IDs, not logins, or your saved data will eventually point at the wrong person.

Missing users are not errors. Looking up a nonexistent username returns a successful response with an empty data array, so handle the empty case explicitly.

Batching exists. The users endpoint takes up to 100 logins in one call, which matters the moment your tool checks lists instead of individuals.

Secrets stay server-side. The client secret identifies your application; calling the token endpoint from browser code hands your app's identity to anyone who opens devtools. Public-facing tools put a small server between the browser and Twitch.

The reason Twitch's third-party ecosystem is so large is that the barrier is so low: one public API, generous free access, and a platform where small questions genuinely matter to people. That is why the space is full of narrow tools that each answer one thing well, when was this account created, is this channel live, how fast is this category growing, which clips popped this week. Most of them are a weekend of work on top of one or two endpoints, and some of them grow into real products.

If you want to start, the path is short: register an application at the developer console, request an app access token, and call the users or streams endpoint for something you actually care about. The official documentation at dev.twitch.tv is current and well maintained, which is not something every platform can claim. Pick one piece of data Twitch collects but does not display, put a clean interface on it, and you are following the same recipe as most of the Twitch tools you already use.

This modder thought opening a window was too much work, so he did something cool about it

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

u/Motor_Attention1865 on Reddit didn't like how his PC added extra heat to his room in the winter, so he went the extra mile to dump the heat outside in a fashion similar to mini-split air conditioners. The external cooling system is controlled by an Arduino Mega that the PC communicates with when it needs extra cooling. The system opens a three-way valve to route coolant outside and prevents condensation by keeping the coolant temperature above the dew point.

Our intrepid modder's room has heated floors, and the PC was dumping too much heat under the table where his PC sits, even in 25 °F (-4 °C) weather. He grew tired of manually opening a window to regulate the temperature in his space, so he put in much more effort to create a split cooling system that puts another radiator outside in the below-freezing temperatures, cooling down the PC significantly.

Motor_Attention1865's build itself is impressive enough, with a delidded Core Ultra 7 270K Plus cooled by a Thermal Grizzly 1851 Mycro Pro direct-die water block with Thermal Grizzly Conductonaut Extreme liquid compound. Not only is his RTX 4070 Ti Super also watercooled with a Bykski water block, but the 2x24GB DDR5-8400 G.Skill RAM is also watercooled using Bykski heat spreaders with an IceManCooler two-channel water block. The cooling system within the PC has two radiators: a 120mm in the back and a 360mm in the front, all fed by an EK Kinetic D5 pump-reservoir.

The external cooling system, however, is even more impressive. The 240mm outdoor radiator with two Noctua iPPC-3000 fans isn’t outrageous, but the automated system that makes it useful is what’s interesting. Next to the PC is a box with a Bykski D5 pump and reservoir that pushes water outside, but it doesn’t use the external radiator until the PC needs the extra cooling.

Upon startup, the PC runs a Python script that communicates with an Arduino Mega connected to three temperature probes checking the coolant temperature and three more temperature and humidity sensors that monitor the PC case and the ambient air. The sensors give the Arduino Mega information on where to switch the motorized three-way valve depending on the temperature and humidity.

The problem with extreme cold in any PC is condensation. If coolant gets below the dew point of the environment, condensation forms, potentially shorting out PC components. To prevent this disaster, the Arduino determines the dew point based on the humidity and temperature of the room and in the PC. Motor_Attention1865 set the Arduino to close off the outside radiator at +10 °C above the dew point, or +5 °C during benchmarking, allowing for low temperatures without risking droplets forming in the PC.

Because of the freezing or below-freezing temperatures at which this external loop is meant to operate, Motor_Attention1865 also added pure ethylene glycol to the Aquacomputer Double Protect Ultra Clear coolant in the loop, lowering its freezing point from -18 °C to -28 °C.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Thanks to the supplemental cooling system and delidding, the system achieves temperatures below 50 °C under heavy use. According to Motor_Attention1865, the RTX 4070 Ti sits at 37 °C and the CPU hovers around 45-50 °C while gaming. Temperatures were higher in benchmarks, however — in Cinebench R23, the CPU sat at 52 °C, while in 3DMark Steel Nomad, the GPU was at 48 °C.

Above all, however, Motor_Attention1865 no longer needs to bother himself with opening a window if their room gets too hot with the PC under load. It's the small things.

#10535. This Texas rocket builder’s high-tech ring of fire could revolutionize aerospace

One early morning in May 2025 at Spaceport America, a desert basin on the outskirts of Las Cruces, New Mexico, a silver rocket shot through the air.

Launches aren’t a rare occurrence at the commercial launch site, but this test flight wasn’t an everyday event. A century after Robert Goddard launched his first liquid-fueled rocket, the flight by Venus Aerospace, a Texas-based startup, may have heralded a new kind of rocket, a new technology, and maybe a new era. 

“It’s a step change in combustion physics,” says Sarah Duggleby, a Venus Aerospace cofounder along with her husband, Andrew Duggleby, a rocket engineer.

The rocket launch represented the first successful U.S. flight of a rotating detonation rocket engine (RDRE). Venus predicts this tech—which harnesses a continuous detonation wave around a ring-shaped chamber, generating increased thrust with less fuel—can achieve hypersonic flight. The startup has seen interest in its technology soar at a time when spending on defense, commercial space development, and aerospace technology is rapidly accelerating. 

Duggleby estimates that Venus RDRE rockets can double the payload that rockets can take into space. 

“It turns out when you build the most efficient liquid rocket engine in the world, defense and space companies start coming to you like, ‘Hey, could you sell us engines?’” she says. “We’ve pivoted, but at the core, it’s always been about, if you want to go fast, you need a new engine.”

The company has raised just shy of $140 million, including a $91 million Series B this June, and employs 113 people, per PitchBook. It struck a development deal with Lockheed Martin this past summer to integrate RDRE tech into precision long-range missiles.

In 2018, Andrew Duggleby was a Navy Reserve officer and the family was stationed in Japan. He and Sarah realized they wouldn’t be able to make it home for a grandmother’s birthday. Andrew joked that while it was going to be an excruciating 13 hours to fly home to the States, there was a new rocket engine technology being developed that could theoretically do the flight in an hour. They laughed, but the idea stuck with them, and they founded Venus two years later. 

The rocket he was talking about was the RDRE. Theorized since the 1980s and finally cracked by a team of researchers from Purdue University and University of Central Florida, RDRE relies on a precisely timed ring of subsonic explosions, calibrated and choreographed to very rapidly detonate in a circular pattern, creating more thrust with less fuel use. 

Traditional rocket engines, from the Saturn V to SpaceX’s Falcon, rely on a combustion process called deflagration, where a flame is exposed to a mixture of fuel and oxidizers. To put it simply: traditional rockets involve a continuous burn, RDRE rockets involve a series of explosions, Sarah Duggleby said an RDRE launch even sounds different; she can tell when a test flight is successful when it hits a certain whistling sound.

Venus’s rockets have achieved 15% more energy efficiency than the Saturn V, the rocket that launched astronauts to the moon in the ‘60s and ‘70s. For comparison, the new SpaceX rockets are just 2% more efficient than their Saturn forebears, Duggleby says. 

The Dugglebys were both working for Virgin Orbit when Sarah read a news item about university researchers proving this new type of engine. In June of 2020, the couple decided to take the leap, quit Virgin, and pursue development of a high-speed plane using this new RDRE technology. 

They chose the Houston Spaceport for the combination of aerospace talent and facilities; currently, from their headquarters at the spaceport, they can test-fire mounted rocket engines right outside their hangar door at Ellington Field. By contrast, Duggleby cited her experience with Virgin and Southern California aerospace, where the developers and startups worked in the South Bay or Long Beach but had to drive hours to test in the Mojave Desert. That added time and cost to development. 

The close physical connection between Venus staff and the test site in Houston has allowed the company to iterate and develop very efficiently, said Duggleby; they developed the new rocket concept in roughly four years with $80 million. 

Along with the theoretical blueprint from researchers, Venus Aerospace needed to engage in extensive testing, as well as materials science experiments and analysis with high-speed cameras, to develop a rocket that was commercially viable. Designing the chamber for the rotating supersonic explosions required deft engineering and new kinds of materials. 

“Here’s an analogy about the challenge of building a rocket,” says Duggleby. “ A rocket’s like lighting a fire in a wax fireplace, and you have to keep the wax from melting.” 

Venus is seeking to develop and test rocket models that can work across defense, space, and aerospace, and devise a manufacturing process to manufacture them at scale. As Duggleby puts it, they’re trying to work with numerous customers to incorporate Venus’s rockets into customers technology, and build a platform to serve all these different industries and engineering challenges. 

“We have a current opportunity with what’s going on geopolitically to get our engine into systems,” she said. “But my hope and dream is that we will . . . not let go of that north star: that this is the engine that will ultimately unlock high-speed global travel.”

#10533. The first and last 3 minutes: How great storytellers win and keep attention

Think about the last business presentation you attended. Chances are the speaker spent hours preparing slides, polishing statistics, and rehearsing the main points. But how did the presentation begin? With a lengthy introduction, a list of credentials, or a few words thanking everyone for attending?

Those opening moments may have cost the speaker the audience’s attention before the presentation even began, and that speaker may have lost the opportunity to make a lasting impression.

After years of speaking to audiences of all sizes, I’ve learned that the first and last three minutes of a presentation deserve more thought than almost anything in between. The opening earns your audience’s attention, while the ending determines what they remember and what they do next.

Your Audience Decides Faster Than You Think

Why the first three minutes? Audiences will decide almost instantly whether to continue giving you their attention or start tuning you out. That’s why I consider the first three minutes—roughly 350 to 400 words at a typical speaking pace—so critical. Your opening must give listeners a reason to keep listening.

An effective opening creates a reason for your audience to stay with you and lean in for more. A strong opening statement can start with something unexpected, a moment of conflict or confusion, a startling discovery, or an intriguing line of dialogue. Your goal is to make your audience want to hear the next sentence.

One of my favorite examples is the story of Dick Hoyt, who refused to give up on his son Rick, born with spastic quadriplegia. When I tell their story, I start with the subject line from an email I received from a friend: “Do not delete this email until you watch this video.” Immediately, the audience wants to know what was in the email and why it mattered. The message introduced me to the extraordinary story of a father who competed in races while pushing his son in a wheelchair. I was so moved and inspired that I wrote a book about them.

Because the first three minutes is so crucial to storytelling success, I recommend memorizing that section. This way, even if things go wrong—and they will go wrong sometimes—you won’t be disoriented or flustered by PowerPoint failures or unexpected noises. Memorizing this key part of your presentation also allows you to be relaxed and in control, since you will appear confident and authoritative instead of reading from a script or fumbling for the next sentence.

KEEP THE AUDIENCE WITH YOU

The opening is essential to capture attention, but the middle is where your audience needs to understand the stakes, care about the people and situations, and—most important—know that you are moving toward something meaningful.

In a business setting, this means making your story relatable. One of my “10 Elements” of storytelling is reversing the I/you ratio. Leaders naturally tell stories from their own perspective: “I did this,” “My company accomplished that,” or “We succeeded.” That leaves the audience wondering, “What does that mean for me?” So instead of saying “I” or “my” or “we,” try to reverse the phrase to be inclusive, saying “you” or “your.” When you help listeners see themselves in your story, they are more likely to remain engaged.

Keeping your audience’s attention also requires you to know where your story is going and how to get there—so you must know the transitions between the sections of your story. You will never be lost, because you always have a frame of reference and can skip seamlessly into the next section.

GREAT ENDINGS DON’T JUST STOP

Just as the first three minutes can make or break your presentation, the final three minutes are equally important. This the culmination of your story, so it is where you should tie up any loose ends and address the questions you have asked or resolve the conflicts you have introduced.

When I finish telling the story of Dick and Rick Hoyt, I return to the special relationship between father and son. I recount asking Rick what he would do if he could use his arms and legs. His answer was simple: He would sit his father in a chair and push him. That moment brings the story full circle. It’s the kind of ending that stays with an audience long after the presentation is over.

In the same way you should memorize the first three minutes of your story, you should also memorize the last three minutes to ensure you don’t stumble over words or get got lost in the middle of a script.

The ending should be definitive, so your audience knows four things:

            1. Your story has ended.

            2. There is a resolution or conclusion. 

            3. The reason for your story is clear.

            4. There is no doubt about the call to action.

The fourth point is essential, because you never want to leave the call to action dangling when you reach the end. Don’t make people guess! If you don’t wrap up the story and hand it to your audience with a bow on top, you’re taking a gamble that they may or may not reach the conclusion you intended.

Your final words should stay with your audience long after they have left the room. This is the ultimate goal of storytelling: to be heard and to make an impact. The next time you prepare an important presentation, remember that the opening governs whether your audience listens, and the ending shapes whether your message resonates.

#10532. Motorola accidentally confirms its ‘Razr Flex’ wide foldable is coming in 2027

Following a past teaser, Motorola has mistakenly posted an early support page that not only confirms the name of its wide foldable as the “Razr Flex,” but also confirms it will be launching in 2027.

The wide foldable trend continues to expand, with Motorola set to launch the “Razr Flex” as its iPhone Duo/Galaxy Z Fold 8 competitor. While there’s been no official announcement, Motorola did directly tease the device around Apple’s launch event, showing it in a silhouette (pictured above).

Now, Motorola has, presumably by accident, confirmed the name and release window of that wide foldable.

A support page on Motorola’s website lists the name of the device as “Razr Flex,” a name we’ve previously heard in connection with this wide form factor, while the page also directly says that the device is a 2027 release. There’s no firm release date, but it’s almost certainly not arriving before the end of the year, despite initial leaks around Motorola’s wide foldable hinting at a 2026 release.

The Motorola “Razr Flex” is expected to have a very compact form factor and, based on Motorola’s initial plans, will likely have 3D glass and at least wants to have a creaseless display, seemingly with just two cameras on the back similar to Apple and Samsung’s wide foldables. The outer display might be a mere 4.97-inch panel, much smaller than others.
