#10531. Box’s Aaron Levie is having fun with AI, and thinks you should, too

Hello again, and welcome back to Fast Company’s Plugged In.

Not long after ChatGPT launched, I visited Box’s Aaron Levie at his office. Looking slightly awed and conspiratorial, the CEO of the collaboration platform showed me a tech experiment he was not yet willing to make public. It involved feeding a business document that was thousands of words long into an LLM. The algorithm quickly ground all that verbiage down into a summary that was concise, clear, accurate . . . and useful.

Suddenly, I could see AI having a profound impact on how knowledge workers got stuff done that went way beyond chatbots. And the fact that Levie thought summarization would matter was one reason I took it seriously.

Levie, who cofounded Box in 2005, has long been one of the tech industry’s clearest thinkers and crispest explainers when it comes to the future of productivity. Lately, reading his Twitter/X commentary on how to best make use of AI is one of the few reasons I still find time to grudgingly lurk on that service.

I recently visited him again to talk about why he posts about AI, how quickly the technology is likely to live up to its potential on an array of fronts, and the ways Box and its customers are putting it to use in their own workflows. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Did you set out to have a Twitter feed that’s dominated by discussion of AI, or did it just happen naturally?

For what it’s worth, this is my happy place, because the amount of awesome stuff happening in technology right now is just kind of amazing. And so the only things I write about are the things that I’m either thinking about, talking to friends about, or seeing from customers or within our business.

It’s a very easy thing to do. I’m just writing as I see it. I’m having an unbelievable amount of fun with everything going on.

To what degree are you trying to frame things so businesses can understand what’s happening and take advantage of it?

It’s interesting. I don’t know if I’m more trying to explain to businesses what’s going on to take advantage of, or explain to Silicon Valley what businesses need to be able to actually use AI.

If I had to guess, two-thirds of the time I’m writing for Silicon Valley and trying to bring tales from the road and reflect on, for instance, why coding adoption is going fully vertical, whereas other forms of knowledge work are diffusing at a slower pace. What’s causing that, and what do we need to think about as a tech industry to better enable that adoption?

A lot of the time, I’m actually more kind of being introspective, on the tech side of the conversation, and that’s what I’m probably mostly doing at the moment.

Is there still a big divide between the Valley and tech companies and startups and the rest of the world?

There is a very big divide, but it’s in axes that are not always 100% predictable. I would say that engineering is probably converging at a faster rate. If you go to a lot of leading banks, and you look at some of their most modern agentic practices around using Cognition or Factory or Cursor or Claude Code, a lot of that might look very similar to what leading companies in Silicon Valley are starting to do. And that’s because engineers generally are pretty tapped into what’s going on.

There’s always 5% of an engineering team that’s super online. They’re paying attention to every new announcement, and then they pull down that new set of best practices, and then that starts to go viral within the organization.

If you’re in a startup, you have a lot more ability to just go. And the person right next to you is maybe the head of IT or the engineer who can help you implement something. Or maybe you’re technical yourself, even if you’re in a marketing or sales role.

The adoption rate tends to actually be faster in the startups by a meaningful amount versus the rest of the world. Large enterprises end up having a lot of compliance, regulatory, and security challenges.

It’s pretty obvious why coding has taken off from a technical standpoint. But what are the most likely candidates for the next things to diffuse?

The capabilities of AI models are quite advanced relative to what we’ve ultimately been able to use them for. And that’s this capability overhang, which basically amounts to, does the rest of the world have some way of connecting the intelligence from these models into a real workflow where they can actually get the gains of that intelligence?

And that’s a hard problem, because if you’re in life sciences and you’re doing massive drug discovery, you might have the world’s most intelligent AI model. But is that AI model able to get access to your proprietary research? Is it able to tap into your clinical drug trial workflow? Are you able to connect it up to all of your various data systems?

If this all happened overnight, it’d be stressful and people wouldn’t have enough time to catch up. But I think we’re in for years of diffusion of AI into these workflows, through an entire applied AI layer of products and companies that go after every single one of these verticals, every single one of these lines of business, and can bridge the model capability with the business process.

You’re going to see them in life sciences. We’ve seen them certainly in legal, with products like Harvey or Legora. We’re going to see them in financial services. We’re going to see them in manufacturing.

And the frontier labs won’t render those specialists irrelevant over time?

The way I think about it approximates most other technologies in history. At almost all times, you have super über-horizontal technologies, and then highly verticalized or specialized tools.

Let’s look at some random examples. If you went backwards 15 years from today, and you looked at the entire product portfolio of AWS and Google Cloud and said, “What do you think the landscape of security products or data service companies or databases or analytics tools will be, given all of the features?” You 100% would not conclude that Snowflake would be a $100 billion company, that Databricks would be a $175 billion company, that ServiceNow would be a $100 billion company, that Palo Alto Networks would be a $250 billion company.

You’d be, like, “Well, wait a second, these gigantic clouds have every feature that every enterprise would ever need for all these services.” It just turns out that that gets you 80% of the way in a lot of the use cases you need to solve. And then the extra 20%, where you just go super deep in a domain, is that applied layer.

They’re not zero-sum. Every dollar that Snowflake or Databricks makes, the underlying cloud providers also make 80 cents of that, or whatever the right number is. That will also be true for AI. The labs will make an unbelievable amount of money based on the applied layer driving workloads through those models. But you still need that bridge layer to be able to connect the workflow into the intelligence.

What advice would you give to knowledge workers who know that AI is important, but are not yet experts, and maybe in some cases are somewhat intimidated by it in terms of what they can do to get value out of it and not be left behind?

You just have to start playing with the tools. And I think people will see a wide range of productivity gain. There are some functions where, even with the best AI in the world, you might only get a 10% or 20% productivity gain. There are some functions—and we’re seeing this with engineering—where you could get a 200% or 300% or 400% productivity gain. But the only way to know where your job function lands, or how to use these tools in the right way, is to adopt them.

The thing that is probably the most interesting—and unnerving to some extent—about this space is you have to keep trying things on an ongoing basis. There are things right now that large percentages of people have written off that AI will not be able to do. And then a new model breakthrough happens, and it finally can do that.

I’d say 90% of the things I do with AI today were not possible two years ago. Somewhere between two years ago and today, there’s been a breakthrough in each of these areas that makes AI more useful, more enjoyable, more effective, more accurate. And I wouldn’t have known that if I didn’t just keep trying and being, like, “Yep, AI is not ready for that use case. I’ll check back in six months.”

How much of Box’s code is being written by AI these days?

Maybe the better stat is that the significant majority of all code that we write has an agent involved in it. I don’t know the percentage of lines, but I would assume it’s the majority of lines written at this point.

I’m 1,000% a believer in agent coding. It’s allowing us to ship way faster. We’re building more features than ever before. We’re solving customer problems way faster. It’s letting us innovate far more than before.

And what does that do to hiring decisions or your general take on how many people you need and what those people will be doing?

I’m inclined to hire more people as a result of AI in most areas. Because if I can increase the productivity of a job function because of AI, and assuming that we don’t have a shortage of things we want to go do, then that just means more output. Which to me translates to more competitiveness, more innovation, more revenue, more opportunities to go serve customers.

Other than a couple of areas, we are firmly on the side of AI as a job creator, and we’re putting our money where our mouth is. We’re still hiring in most job areas right now, and that will continue to be the case.

Other than coding, how are people using AI within Box?

Kind of for everything, across people’s jobs. One of the benefits of Box itself as a company is nearly all of our data is in Box. It creates an automatic knowledge base for everything you’d want to know: project status, onboarding, a new sales rep who needs to learn how to sell our product, decisions that we made two years ago that now have an implication in some new thing that we’re doing. Product architecture, strategy, all your classic knowledge work use cases of learning about the business and being able to accelerate projects.

That’s how we use it day to day. And then people use ChatGPT and they use Claude for a bunch of other kind of workflows.

How’s the cost? Are people tokenmaxxing and bankrupting you?

We never leaned into the tokenmaxxing side. Nor have we leaned into “You must justify all of your AI usage.” We think people are going to be adults about this. Especially for engineering, we have very disciplined product road maps. And so almost by definition, if we agree on the product road map, then we actually would want to build that product as fast as possible.

So then definitionally you would spend as much money as you could, assuming you could afford it, to get that product done as quickly as possible. And to whatever extent AI can accelerate that in a safe way and a robust way, we want to go and do that.

What should people be worried about with AI?

I think people have an initial relatively myopic view of automation, which is, well, obviously companies are going to use automation to get rid of people. And what I actually find in working with customers is that they mostly want automation so they can accelerate their business on whatever dimension is valuable to their company.

If you’re in life sciences, you want to accelerate drug discovery and clinical drug trials. If you’re in banking, you want to accelerate client onboarding. If you’re in engineering, you want to accelerate software development.

Most companies don’t make that much money by saving money and then just making that into profit. You often can make money by saving money and then redeploying those saved dollars to something else. But then what you usually redeploy them to is also a thing that has labor and has people involved in it. The reason I tend to be pretty optimistic is because when I spend time with customers, they’re optimistic, and they’re not doing the dystopian things that I think people imagine companies are doing with this technology.

The reality is that most companies are saying, “Hey, if you can make my employees 20% more productive, that doesn’t mean I get rid of 20% of my employees. It means I’m going to fight like hell to be even more competitive in my market, to generate more leads and be able to better serve customers and build more features and get more intelligence about the market that I’m in.”

That’s ultimately what I’m seeing play out in a lot of customer environments. And we’re seeing the same thing within our own business.

#10526. The war on polyester is coming for your underwear. One brand’s answer? Wool

Back when she was too young to buy her own clothes, Kerry O’Brien remembers loathing hefty wool sweaters—especially turtlenecks. But her career as the founder and CEO of basics brand Commando gave her a new perspective on fabrics and fibers, including a love for wool and what can be done with it beyond creating itchy knitwear. Now, decades after her turtleneck terrors, O’Brien brought wool to unexpected new territory: panties. 

Commando started out nearly 25 years ago by transferring some of the fabrics engineered for activewear to women’s intimates, originally building a brand on seamless, raw-cut panties made of a synthetic fabric. But the new wool panties, which are available online now and in select stores and retail for $38, inherently achieve a lot of what those nylon panties do artificially.

“Nothing can really replicate the technical aspects of wool, what it does naturally,” O’Brien tells Fast Company. 

This wool underwear debut coincidentally comes amid some consumers’ growing war on polyester, which also happens to be the most produced fiber on the planet.

Abercrombie, for instance, recently drew controversy online over a mostly synthetic women’s sweater marketed as a “wool-blend.” More broadly, a growing number of fashion content creators are lauding the benefits of natural fibers over synthetics, citing environmental and health concerns. (So are wellness and MAHA influencers, although a direct, causal connection between microplastics and sickness has yet to be proven). “Polyester” has even become an insult among Gen Z.

This consumer preference is also showing up in search trends. Interest in “natural fibers” is up 60% over the past year alone, according to Google Trends. Zoom out further, and stats show the term is up a whopping 140% over the past five years.

Wool panties aren’t a new invention; they’ve historically been sold at wool-focused brands and more niche outerwear labels. But they might be on the horizon of becoming a more mainstream, fashion-forward panty as synthetic pushback continues.

Why wool?

Despite its often scratchy connotations, this fiber that most commonly comes from sheep has a lot of natural advantages. For example, it possesses abilities in “moisture management, biodegradability, renewability, temperature regulation, and odor resistance,” Huipu Gao, PhD, an assistant professor of textile development at the Fashion Institute of Technology, says. These properties lend themselves well to women’s underwear, especially moisture management, odor resistance, and temperature regulation. 

“[Wool] is the next frontier,” O’Brien says. “Everybody has a wool sweater. Everybody knows what wool is. Unfortunately, they have this idea that wool has to be chunky, scratchy, super warm, and thick.” But it can be altered the same way cotton can, to become everything from Kleenex to a hefty sweatshirt. As shoppers increasingly look for natural fibers, wool might be an emerging contender, including in the women’s underwear space where cotton has long reigned as the recommended and most available fabric. 

Why wool has its challenges

The reason why wool probably hasn’t taken off as a go-to material choice for undergarments has less to do with make than with cost, according to Gao, who noted that fine wool fibers are more expensive. Wool also requires additional treatments in order to prevent pilling and shrinking when washed and dried, which add to the overall bill. Altogether, added requirements and their subsequent added costs have likely limited its popularity in underwear thus far, he says.

Transforming wool also comes with difficulties. For luxury hosiery, intimates, and apparel brand Wolford—which launched a six-silhouette capsule (sans panties) in collaboration with Australia-based wool certification and advocacy group Woolmark in early October—the challenge began with developing the right yarn.

It took a lot of trial and error to “find the right balance in the micron of the fiber and the twist” to create a super soft fabric that’d feel comfortable on the skin, Wolford CEO Marco Pozzo says. In other words, they had to figure out the right diameter of the fiber to use (measured in microns) and the right tautness of the yarn’s twist, without it breaking or creating something uncomfortable on the skin. 

“The other challenge was the finishing and the dyeing because the reaction to the color was very different on natural fiber compared to the synthetic fiber,” Pozzo says. “Every sheep is different, like our hair, so the way they absorb the color can be very different.” 

Wolford had to change its dye “recipe,” especially to recreate its signature colors. To finish things, Pozzo says they “stabilized the material in a steam chamber” to prevent the fabric from performing differently or changing sizes across variable environments, be they cold, hot, or humid.

Liz Sargent, fibers professor at the Savannah College of Art and Design School of Fashion, explains that fiber fineness is the key to spinning wool comfortably enough to work as underwear or a first layer. “Merino fibers are extremely fine, which lets them bend easily rather than poke the skin. That flexibility is why merino can feel as soft as cashmere and as smooth as silk against the body,” she says, adding that “next-to-skin Merino” usually ranges between 15.5 and 18.5 microns. For items like underwear that need recovery or bounce back to their original shape, she says, “wool is often blended with or wrapped around a small amount of nylon or elastane.”

Why brands keep using elastane

The blend Sargent describes is what’s in Wolford’s line, which uses one pure wool fabric and one with 15% elastane mixed in. It’s also what’s in Commando’s French cut panty, which is composed of 96% wool and 4% elastane. With that sprinkle of synthetic, the new Commando panty isn’t pure natural fiber, but O’Brien wanted it this way, regardless of current backlash. 

“[Elastane] is really a key ingredient to Commando, helping things stretch and be modulus against your body,” she says. Wool naturally has stretch to it, but it can shrink and warp out of its original shape depending on heat and agitation. Elastane makes that bounce-back after a wear or machine wash possible. That’s why O’Brien cautions against completely ditching synthetics. 

“Synthetic fabrics have given us a lot of benefits over the years in terms of technical performances,” she says. That being said, the CEO is also leaning into more natural fibers ahead. Within the next year, Commando plans to release new lines made with cashmere and linen, each with a fraction of elastane mixed in.

Wolford is also thinking about its natural fiber evolution. Though the initial wool line only features ready-to-wear garments, Pozzo is tracking how it sells in order to decide whether Wolford should add silhouettes—including, possibly, wool panties.

#10525. Yuri Suzuki’s ‘Onomatopia’ is a mini theme park designed to be listened to

Sound artist, designer, and electronic musician Yuri Suzuki uses ambient noise and miniature rides inspired by theme park attractions to explore the connections between play, sound, and architecture in his new exhibition Onomatopia.

On display through January 7, 2027, in the Osh Gallery at Pentagram’s London headquarters, the exhibition includes five dioramas based on amusement park attractions, world fairs, and expos. It’s a prototype of a theme park built around one’s sense of hearing, as each ride makes its own specific noises. The park in total is designed to evoke a greater appreciation for the role of sound.

Suzuki is a former Pentagram partner who designed a logo for the musical standard MIDI that’s both visual and sonic, and his Ambient Machine lets you customize your own white noise. He’s also designed public multisensory artwork, including for the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and a Sonic Playground for Atlanta’s High Museum of Art.

Suzuki’s latest work continues to explore those ideas. There’s a mini roller coaster called “Harmony in Motion” with horns in red, yellow, blue, and green in varying heights sprouting around the tracks, which sound like an organ playing in harmony. A red, yellow, and blue Ferris wheel display named “Mechanical Music Wheel” makes the sound of bright rising and falling chimes.

A bumper cars attraction makes irregular plucking sounds. And there’s a sonic carousel and helter-skelter, each made from multicolored horns. Suzuki tells Fast Company he tends to use primary colors because they are accessible.

“Even color blind people can see the difference in the color,” he says. At the same time, the primary and secondary colors visually simplify what otherwise looks complicated in his work of twisting shapes and horns.

“Sometimes my installation looks very complicated . . . like lots of pipes coming together. But if you divide it by color, it’s a clear division,” he says.

His work is bright and interactive; a jungle gym of horns inviting the public to listen and play, and it’s inspired by the worldbuilding of Disney and theme parks. He says he’s long been fascinated by the idea of theme parks or expos that express the ideal city, or utopia, especially Walt Disney and Epcot (Disney’s “experimental prototype community of tomorrow”).

“Sound is invisible,” Suzuki tells Fast Company, which makes it hard to notice how it affects your life. It can be used toward negative ends, like a sonic weapon, or for positive ends, like, say, a theme park for your ears. He says sound design is often a low priority compared to other disciplines like visual and product design, but it’s actually “very impactful.”

The Onomatopia dioramas are on display along with reference materials from Suzuki’s own collection, like a 2001 Disney World map for its 40th anniversary. The exhibition, co-curated with Vicky Richardson, builds on Suzuki’s past work, including last year’s Coaster of Sounds at the Royal Academy Summer Exhibition. It’s a miniature version of what he hopes is one day a full-scale park with sound wellness designed into its experience—his own Epcot or World Expo to draw attention to the power of sound in human communication.

Suzuki says Onomatopia is meant to provide visitors a landscape of escape that ultimately allows them to look back at reality and consider how they want the world to be.

The data center boom is negatively affecting Ukraine's war effort.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine sparked a new era of drone warfare. Russian invaders first used drones with fiber-optic tethers to combat electronic warfare on the front lines, but both sides now use these jam-proof drones. Against that backdrop, the AI data center buildout is making it harder for Ukraine to buy the fiber-optic spools that it needs to continue scaling its drone manufacturing capabilities. A research and development representative for BlueBird Tech, a Ukrainian defense firm specializing in drones, told Ars Technica in an interview that prices of fiber optic cables have risen around six to 10 times in the past couple of years as AI data center demand soaks up more and more of the supply of this resource.

According to that interview, It’s estimated that Ukraine and Russia are producing around 50,000 fiber optic drones monthly, with each drone capable of ranges of up to 62 miles. But Ukraine has only been able to acquire 72 miles of fiber optic cable from Chinese suppliers during August 2025, whereas Russia imported a whopping 328,000 miles during that same month. It was estimated that Russia acquired 37 million miles of fiber during the entirety of 2025, accounting for over 10% of the global production.

What makes matters worse for Ukrainian defenders is that there is an estimated 111-million-mile shortfall in fiber optic cable supply across the world, adding to the various shortages that the data center industry has faced in recent years. Aside from the material shortfall, Ukraine faces trade barriers in acquiring more fiber. The BlueBird representative claimed that some Chinese companies have outright refused to sell Ukraine fiber optic cables.

China is the primary supplier of this material, so it’s easier for Russia to obtain them through its massive land border with the country. While Ukraine could purchase fiber optic cables from suppliers located in other countries, that's not much of an alternative. The BlueBird rep notes: "there can be intermediaries in other countries, and prices can differ depending on the country and the purchasing route. But in the end, China remains the main source of the fiber optic material we are talking about.”

There has also been talk of producing fiber optic cables domestically in Ukraine, but such manufacturing requires specially trained personnel who must practice on the already limited supply of fiber optic cables. Even if manufacturers automate production, they still require experienced personnel who can oversee the line and ensure the quality of the final product.

The data center build out has been causing all kinds of shortages. We’ve seen supply shortfalls in GPUs, memory chips, and even PCBs, but there’s also shortages in other seemingly unrelated industries like power infrastructure, optical transceivers, and even in critical skilled labor like electricians. This overwhelming demand has started affecting other industries not related to computing, like cars, home construction, and now, fiber optic attack drones.

#10521. The federal government wants you to use its chatbot to report fraud

The Trump administration has added a new fraud-reporting tool to the federal government’s official chatbot.

America.gov launched in September as a centralized online hub for official government information. Created by the National Design Studio, it’s meant to streamline communication for the AI age. The site’s home page has a prompt box that answers questions based on a model trained on government websites and sources. Now, the site’s newest user interface update shows how America.gov is mirroring the administration’s messaging.

Designers added a pill button below the prompt box on America.gov to “Report government fraud” late last month. Click through, and users are taken to a page with two options: to either report benefits fraud for Medicaid, Medicare, unemployment, or Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, (formerly known as food stamps), or to report voter fraud. The “About” pages for the reporting processes say reports are encrypted and your name is optional, but it offers the possibility of cash rewards for those who include contact information.

America.gov’s new prompt functionality comes amid Trump’s growing focus on fraud, and following the launch of fraud.gov in August, a site that uses inflated figures to claim the Trump administration has uncovered hundreds of billions of dollars in fraud in his second term. (The New York Times found the administration’s figures included temporary funding pauses, cases that predated his second term, and claims that hadn’t been verified.) Trump wrote on his social network Thursday that he was directing Vice President JD Vance to “focus his complete and total attention” on crime and corruption in cities and states controlled by Democrats.

The Trump administration’s approach to fighting fraud targets high volume, low-dollar cases in states that didn’t vote for him or his party. That high volume could make for quick, easy wins that the administration may point to as proof it’s successfully fighting fraud and to build a narrative of poorly run Democrat-led states.

At the same time, it comes as many wealthy and well-connected fraudsters have gotten off the hook in Trump’s second term thanks to his pardons and his administration’s crime-fighting priorities.

Trump’s Department of Justice (DOJ) is bringing fewer white-collar cases forward than his predecessors, according to a review by Justice Connection, a group of former DOJ employees. Meanwhile, Trump’s presidential pardons have cost American taxpayers and crime victims about $1.3 billion in restitution and payments, according to Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee. House Democrats say they will investigate Trump’s so-called “pardon economy” and possible conflicts of interest when the next Congress begins in 2027.

America.gov’s “Report government fraud” button puts Trump’s fraud-fighting strategy front and center on the government’s chatbot. It was added ahead of other planned updates, like a future integration with Login.gov, a single sign-on service, that the National Design Studio considers part of its phase two for the chatbot.

Early America.gov users found that America.gov correctly answered questions about things like climate change and the 2020 election results, undercutting Trump’s false claims on those topics and passing an early test of the chatbot’s ability to be accurate and neutral. The new button shows, however, that the administration is more than happy to use suggested prompts and user journeys to promote Trump’s priorities and messaging.

#10520. Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

LangSmith is closed-source and restricts self-hosting to enterprise licenses, teams that run their own LLMOps stack and want to keep traces on their own servers need an alternative. To find the best fit, we set a baseline by tracing a small TypeScript agent (equipped with two tools) in LangSmith Cloud. Then, we ran the exact same agent through Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, Opik, and AcruxCore using each platform's recommended TypeScript setup. All tests were run on November 5, 2026, and we pulled every trace back through each tool's API to verify the data.

All four alternatives successfully recreated LangSmith’s trace tree for the test prompt: a single agent span containing three LLM calls and two tool calls. The real differences between them come down to how much boilerplate code you have to write, how spans are typed, whether costs are tracked, and the overall server footprint.

Why Teams Look for a LangSmith Alternative

LangSmith remains the best choice if you already use LangChain and allow cloud hosting—it required just 25 lines of code in our test. The alternatives below are for teams that don't fit that profile.

To test these platforms, we built a simple customer support agent equipped with two tools:

Both tools use static fixture data to ensure every test run is identical. The agent runs a standard loop: it prompts the model, executes any requested tools, and stops once the model provides a final answer.

We tested the agent with three specific prompts to see how the tracing handled different levels of complexity:

For our comparison, we focused entirely on the third question because it generates a robust, multi-step trace.

Under the hood, the agent uses the standard openai package to call the qwen3.8-flash model. We originally picked this model based on its reliable tool-calling behavior during early probing thought it once skipped a tool call later.

We used LangSmith as our baseline. By tracing the agent there first, we created a checklist of every field it captured, and we judged all the alternatives against that exact list.

For setup, we followed the recommended TypeScript approach from each tool's documentation. Phoenix didn't have specific instructions for using its register() helper with OpenAI in TypeScript, so we adapted the pattern from their Anthropic guide.

Here is the agent with no tracing. Each tool section adds one tracing file that imports these files and changes nothing in them.

LangSmith traces the plain openai package with two helpers. wrapOpenAI records each model call, and traceable records your own functions. Without traceable on the run and the tools, wrapOpenAI alone gave three separate root runs and no tool runs.

This file adds 25 lines and removes 3, and installs one package.

LangSmith showed one root run with five children in call order: LLM, get_order_status, LLM, get_refund_policy, LLM. Every field it recorded became a row of the checklist table under "Results". Cost appeared only after a custom price entry. In our error run the failing tool was marked as an error, but the root stayed success: traceable turned the throw into a rejected promise that our agent did not await, so the agent carried on and answered.

Langfuse self-hosts as six containers, including ClickHouse, a column store built for large scans. In our measurement the stack held 2.60–2.64 GiB of memory at idle. Its Docker Compose guide recommends at least 4 CPU cores and 16 GiB RAM, with about 100 GiB of disk.

The TypeScript path is built on OpenTelemetry. You start the OTel Node SDK with LangfuseSpanProcessor, wrap the client with observeOpenAI, and wrap your own functions with observe:

This file adds 31 lines and removes 5, and installs four packages. We pinned the OTel Node SDK to 0.223.0, because @langfuse/otel 6.1.1 does not accept 0.300.0.

Langfuse successfully recreated the same trace tree, neatly tagging the spans as AGENT, GENERATION, and TOOL. It captured all the essentials: tool calls, tool definitions, and the complete message history. However, for the LLM output, it only saved the assistant's message—dropping the finish_reason, response ID, and the provider name.

We ran our deployment in Langfuse v4's events_only mode, which turns off the v1 trace endpoint. Because of this, the API didn't return a centralized trace object or root-level sums for tokens and costs, even though the UI calculated and displayed them perfectly (we didn't test other modes).

Costs showed up exactly as expected once we added a custom price entry. Since Langfuse calculates prices based on the specific usage types you define, and we only set rates for input and output, the separate reasoning tokens went unpriced. Finally, during our error test, the observe wrapper let the error bubble up to the agent, correctly flagging both the tool and the root span as an ERROR.

Phoenix self-hosts as two containers, one Python server and Postgres. In our measurement it held 0.47 GiB at idle. Phoenix is source-available under the Elastic License 2.0, so it is not open source. Authentication is off until you turn it on.

The TypeScript path uses Phoenix's register() helper and the OpenInference instrumentation for the OpenAI package. OpenInference is a set of OpenTelemetry attribute names for LLM spans. traceAgent and traceTool wrap the run and the tools:

This file adds 32 lines and removes 3, and installs three packages.

Phoenix rebuilt the same tree, typed as AGENT, LLM and TOOL. Each LLM span keeps the full OpenAI response object, plus the messages as flattened attributes. The root span stores no token count, but Phoenix computes a sum for the root and the trace when you read it. Cost and those sums are only in the GraphQL API and the UI, and the REST API has no per-trace endpoint.

Cost appeared after a custom price entry under Settings > Models, and Phoenix priced the reasoning tokens by falling back to the output price. In the error run, the tool span and the root were marked ERROR, and the tool span carried an exception event with the stack trace.

Opik self-hosts as eight containers, including ClickHouse, MySQL and ZooKeeper. In our measurement it held 3.69 GiB at idle, the most of the four. The self-hosted UI opened without a login, so every trace was readable from any machine that could reach the port.

The TypeScript path wraps the client with trackOpenAI and your own functions with track. By default trackOpenAI starts a new trace for every model call, so the file passes the run's span through the documented parent option:

This file adds 33 lines and removes 5. It installs opik-openai 2.2.142, and npm adds opik 1.11.14 as its peer, because opik-openai asks for opik ^1.8.61.

Opik successfully recreated the trace tree, and its trace object neatly tallies token counts across all LLM spans. In the logs, tool arguments are bundled into an array, and the LLM output only retains the assistant's message.

We did notice a quirk with the documented OpenAI wrapper (tested on the npm package opik 1.11.14): it tags model calls as general rather than llm, which incorrectly leaves the llm_span_count at zero. (We didn't test newer Opik core versions to see if this has changed). Additionally, because our synchronous tools execute in under a millisecond, they log the exact same start time as the subsequent LLM call, causing the UI to list the LLM call first out of order.

Cost tracking is entirely manual. Opik showed no costs by default, and the documentation doesn't mention a custom price table. We checked the configuration tabs on our 2.2.52 instance (Feedback definitions, AI Providers, Workspace preferences) and found no model pricing settings. To see costs, you have to manually assign a price to each individual span yourself—only the spans we hardcoded this way displayed a cost.

Finally, error reporting is highly detailed. If something fails, Opik attaches an error_info block—complete with the error type, message, and full traceback—directly to the tool span, the root span, and the overall trace.

AcruxCore self-hosts as five containers: Postgres, Redis, a Node API and worker, and nginx. In our measurement it held 0.39 GiB at idle, the least of the four. Its quickstart leaves sign-up open and ships a committed default GATEWAY_ENCRYPTION_KEY, which encrypts stored provider keys; replace it. We tested a local build from 2026-09-17.

The TypeScript path AcruxCore's docs put first is its gateway. The official openai client keeps working: you point its baseURL at ACRUXCORE_BASE_URL + "/gateway" and call a model registered in AcruxCore, which forwards each call to an OpenAI-compatible provider. The gateway records every model call as an llm span. The SDK's step helpers add the rest: traces.step opens the agent span, traces.wrap wraps each tool, and two headers file the gateway's spans under the agent span:

This file adds 30 lines and removes 5, and installs one package. It builds its own client, so it does not use provider.ts. The gateway refused our team API key, so the client uses a gateway virtual key created in the dashboard.

On this path every model call passes through the AcruxCore server, which none of the other four tools need. If you do not want a proxy in the request path, the SDK's register() helper sends OpenTelemetry spans from your process instead. On that path the step helpers do not join the openai package's spans, so you write the agent and tool spans by hand.

AcruxCore rebuilt the same tree, typed as agent, llm and tool, in call order. Each LLM span keeps the full response, the provider and the cached-token count, and the trace carries a token total. The LLM spans do not keep the tool definitions sent to the model, and no reasoning-token count was recorded. The trace took its name from the question, not from the agent span, and each LLM span is named by its start time.

Cost appeared on every LLM span and as a sum on the trace, from the custom price we set on the model in AcruxCore's model list. In the error run, the step helpers marked the tool span and the agent root as error with the error message, with no status code of ours. The API returned no stack trace.

All five tools accept traces over OTLP, the OpenTelemetry wire format. trace-otel.ts sends the same spans with no vendor package: the OTel Node SDK, the OTLP/HTTP protobuf exporter and the OpenInference OpenAI instrumentation. The exporter reads its endpoint and headers from environment variables:

We ran the two-tool question once per backend and changed only environment variables: the endpoint, the headers, and for Phoenix a resource attribute that sets the project name (without it, spans go to a default project). "Accepted" means the exporter reported success, which it does only for an HTTP 2xx, and we read the spans back through each API.

Opik stored the root and tool spans as general although AGENT and TOOL kinds were sent; the cause is Not tested. LangSmith mapped AGENT to its chain type. If you instrument with plain OTel and OpenInference attributes, your raw spans are not tied to one vendor, but span types, cost and trace views still differ by backend.

The first table covers setup: how much server each tool needs, how much code we changed in the agent, and how cost and the plain OTel exporter worked. Phoenix and AcruxCore had the smallest servers, and AcruxCore needed the fewest lines among the self-hosted tools. Opik was the only one without a price table.

The second table checks each trace against what LangSmith recorded for the same run, one field at a time. All five rebuilt the same tree with tokens and durations. They differ in span types, how much of the LLM output they keep, where token sums live, and how much detail they store for the failing tool.

Token totals for the two-tool question ranged from 1,910 to 2,111. Each tool traced a separate run and reasoning length varies, so these numbers do not compare the tools.

All five tools successfully traced our test agent, so the right choice really comes down to your team's specific constraints, infrastructure preferences, and how tracing fits into the rest of your MLOps tooling.

All four alternatives successfully recreated LangSmith’s trace tree. The real deciding factors are boilerplate code, span typing, cost tracking, and server bloat.

LangSmith remains the simplest option for LangChain users who can utilize the cloud. Otherwise, your choice depends on your priorities: Langfuse for community size, Phoenix for a lightweight Postgres footprint, Opik for strict Apache-2.0 compliance with deep error logging, or AcruxCore for combined tracing and tool governance on minimal hardware. Best of all, if you stick to standard OpenTelemetry spans, you aren't locked in—you can try them all and easily pivot later.

#10518. Samsung bets that you’ll either buy a Galaxy S27 Pro or Ultra next year

Samsung is teeing up to kick off 2027 with an all-new lineup of flagship smartphones, and despite rising prices at your local Best Buy, the brand is still hedging that you’re going to pony up for the most premium model available.

As reported by ETNews, Samsung is currently allotting over 70 percent of its total production capabilities to just the Galaxy S27 Ultra and the new Galaxy S27 “Pro” model expected to launch alongside it. That leaves the plain Galaxy S27 and the larger S27+ on the outside looking in. In comparison to this year’s launch, the Galaxy S26 Ultra made up about 50 percent of this series’ production volume, for a grand total of 18 million units.

Historical performance implies Samsung is probably correct here. While big displays are typically what consumers are drawn to, it does appear that the S27 Pro won’t be all that much smaller than the S27+. Considering the Pro should slot in right around the typical price point as the Plus model, it’s not hard to imagine plenty of would-be S27+ buyers moving to the Pro.

For what it’s worth, Samsung betting big on high-end devices usually pays off. We’re on year two of the Fold series seeing big successes — first with the redesigned Fold 7 in 2025, then with the reshaped Fold 8 this year — and the Galaxy S26 Ultra managed to become the best-selling Android phone in Q2 of this year in a list typically populated by iPhones and cheap Galaxy A-series models. Even with prices constantly on the rise, the people yearn for flagship smartphones. You just have to wonder where that ceiling actually is.

#10517. ‘It tends to tick people off’: How the U.S.’s biggest news union is fighting an AI onslaught

A decade ago, while working as a data reporter at the Los Angeles Times, Jon Schleuss watched a new boss take control of the paper’s parent company, rename it Tronc, and promise to supercharge the business by repackaging the paper’s “content” across an array of media. Instead, leadership began “running it into the ground,” says Schleuss. “We decided to fight.” He soon helped organize the newsroom’s first union. Now, as president of the NewsGuild-CWA, the largest news union in the United States, Schleuss is hearing a new version of the same story, this time powered by AI.

Case in point is USA Today Co., formerly Gannett, the country’s largest newspaper chain. In August, the company announced a partnership with Palantir—the data analytics giant whose clients include Nvidia, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Britain’s National Health Service—to better monetize its audience and content. It’s part of a broader effort that includes push-button videos, AI-written article summaries, and even whole articles. That sort of automation echoes moves across the media industry.

NewsGuild members at USA Today papers have demanded an end to the Palantir deal, citing reader trust and a conflict of interest for reporters who cover ICE. The union has also pushed back on some of the company’s artificial intelligence initiatives amid continuing layoffs. Last month, after the rollout of a new reader-facing chatbot across USA Today websites, guild journalists at two papers in Ohio pulled their bylines; among its hallucinations, they said, the bot misidentified the reporter covering a murder case as the suspect.

In an interview in September, Mike Reed, the USA Today CEO, told Fast Company that the company won’t replace journalists with AI. But unlike Ziff Davis, IGN, The New Republic, Time, and CalMatters, it hasn’t put that promise in a contract—something that NewsGuild journalists are now demanding in ongoing negotiations.

The layoffs keep coming, too, even in cases where contracts include AI protections. (The Local Journalist Index estimates that the U.S. has lost about 80% of its local journalists since the turn of the century, from about 40 per 100,000 residents in 2002 to just 7.8 today.)

But the upheaval is also fueling an organizing surge, one Schleuss says the union hasn’t seen since its founding in 1933 as the American Newspaper Guild, during the Great Depression. In the time that he has been president, the guild has added more than 10,000 workers from 246 workplaces—not just journalists but people in the publishing, tech, and nonprofit worlds. (Reporters at Fast Company and Inc. unionized with the Writers Guild of America East in 2018.) “You see CEOs that make millions of dollars and don’t increase your pay and want to lay you off and speak in this weird, AI-written code-speak,” Schleuss says. “It tends to tick people off when the price of groceries is just through the roof.”

Schleuss spoke with Fast Company about the industry’s embrace of AI, the growing labor movement in journalism, and what it will take to protect reporters—and the work they do. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Generative AI is being rolled out all over the place, from healthcare to hiring to scammy content creating. Why is the discussion about AI in journalism so critical?

The news industry is the only industry mentioned in the Constitution—we can start there. A free press is essential to having a democracy, and so if you replace the workers who provide that free press with bots, you get misinformation. 

Our currency is trust. And you can’t do that if you’ve got corporations that are just spewing out word calculators to replace those working journalists who have ethical responsibilities: seeking truth and reporting it, minimizing harm, acting accountable and independent, and being transparent. Those are all our key ethical concerns, and if we stray from them too far, then we lose faith, we lose trust, we lose our free press, we lose our democracy. So I’d say it’s all a pretty straight through line: Without journalists, we don’t have democracies, and replacing journalists with AI is a very quick way to get rid of the democracy. Which might be a goal.

Let’s start with USA Today Co., formerly Gannett, the biggest newspaper chain. How are journalists there seeing AI get rolled out in its newsrooms?

They’re pushing AI on people. One tool, Espresso, will take a press release and then try to spit out a story. But I don’t know, it seems really dangerous if the Nazis are emailing you a press release and you just make a quote-unquote story about it. They’re also trying to do that instead of hiring humans to write a story. So it becomes this one-sided slop that journalists are then forced to edit in as quick an amount of time as possible.

That’s not exactly journalism.

You have to approach AI with journalistic ethics, which I think is Gannett’s real problem. And that’s been the challenge all along: How do you make sure that we are doing the things necessary as journalists to be ethical when we’re using these systems? And that requires seeking the actual truth and reporting it, and not just relying on the output from a single-sourced community news announcement that was emailed to you. It requires actually fact-checking things. That requires going through any data that’s being analyzed to verify that these things that you’re saying are true.

Fact-checking is already a heavy lift. And more AI often means more checking. With fewer journalists and more AI, don’t we risk automating away the very things that we need to make the AI work? To make facts and society work. It’s like, remember why we are doing this to begin with. Why we are reading things.

Do you remember when the company Tronc was created? That was my life. I lived and worked for the L.A. Times, which was owned by Tronc. And its chairman at the time, Michael Ferro, was like, “We’re just going to put the content in different funnels.” It’s basically, I think, what [USA Today CEO] Mike Reed’s strategy is today. And it was a failed strategy. It’s like he doesn’t think about the work that journalists do as telling stories. He thinks of it as content. This is the thing that is just so broken to so many media executives. They think of content; they don’t think of stories. It’s absolutely tone deaf and 10 years old.

The thing that infuriates me: You go to any of the USA Today websites now, and the websites are broken. I wish that he would spend more time working on actual user interfaces. Try not to have so many ads that are autoplaying, because if you’re a reader and you’re trying to read the news, you are holding onto a bucking bronco trying to follow the words on the screen. Everything’s moving around so fast. 

To me, the crux of the issue is: This is all about trust with readers. And if you align yourself with a very shady and dark company that has actively supported an agency that has hurt journalists, your readers are not going to trust you as much. And the latest polling shows that 52% of Americans are more concerned about AI than excited about it. It just seems such a bad move, when trust in journalism’s already at such a record low, for a journalism organization to then lean into AI. 

What else do you think USA Today’s leaders are getting wrong? And how is the union responding?

There’s the part of his interview with you where Mike Reed says AI won’t replace journalists: “I think the Guild plants this, as well as outside cynics, that we’re going to replace journalists with AI. That couldn’t be further from the truth.” But the reality is, we have 95 contracts [across the union] that have AI language in them, and the best-case-scenario ones say the employer will not lay off workers because of AI. But Gannett has refused to agree to any of that language. 

What’s the status of those conversations now? 

We’ve got 46 different contracts at Gannett, so it depends on where each of them are. They’re still bargaining for a first contract at The Columbus Dispatch—they just unionized this year. But everyone’s been fighting for no layoffs because of AI. Mike Reed’s refused to agree to that, but then they’ve also actually laid people off. 

What’s some of the most interesting AI-related language you’ve seen in other newsroom contracts?

What’s one of the funnest ones that’s super simple? The New Republic in December of ’24, says: “Generative AI may be used by bargaining unit employees as a complementary tool in editorial work, but it may not be used as a primary tool for creation of such. The use of AI shall not result in the layoff of a bargaining unit employee, be used to avoid filling any vacant bargaining unit position, or result in an employee’s compensation decreasing.” 

There was also a lefty magazine, The American Independent, and its contract said, simply: “Employees shall not use AI to produce any published material, with the exception of quotes derived from interview transcripts . . . or shall not utilize or approve the use of AI to produce editorial content for publication.” It was aggressive. 

What is the guild aiming for generally in its contracts?

The five major points that we fight for in contracts are: 

Number one is no layoffs because of AI. 

Number two is no salary reductions because of AI—another thing that Gannett has refused to agree to. 

Number three is usually the formation of a labor-management committee so that issues can be worked out in real time. This has been, frankly, really successful and could be successful at Gannett, but journalists there have kept away from it.

Number four is just making sure that you don’t do any impersonation of journalists. Don’t train off of their work or impersonate them without their permission. 

And the fifth and final one is really important for our readers: If you’re going to use AI to generate something, you need to label it.

When we spoke, Reed made it sound like that was a policy, that they would be clear if they were using AI.

The policy is adorable, but it’s not legally binding. It’s the AI language you actually want in a collective bargaining agreement—because if you don’t have a union, then you get no say. 

What they typically push for from the management side is saying something like, “AI may be used to generate news content that is supplementary to local news reporting and is not a replacement for it.” And then they’ll say, “The use of AI by all parties shall be consistent with the ethical guidelines and policies for Gannett journalists regarding AI-generated or assisted content.” But there’s nothing, at least in these contracts that I’m looking at, that says anything about labeling. So it might be in that guideline that they put out, but again, if they can just change that, they will. 

There’s a really good bill that’s sitting on [Governor] Kathy Hochul’s desk in New York called the New York FAIR News Act. It would require labeling for anything that was wholly generated using AI on a news website. Publishers are freaking out about it. They’re like, “Well, this is a violation of the 1st Amendment.” In 1933, whenever you didn’t want journalists to organize a union, you claimed the 1st Amendment protected you. But you have to put terms of service on [your website]. You have to have a privacy policy on your website. Labeling AI content on your news website shouldn’t be bad. It seems basic. 

What happens when AI gets better at simulating journalism, and the disclaimers disappear?

It’s already gotten better at writing, but the problem is, I think, people have also gotten better at seeing it. And even if it’s like, “Is this Coke or is this Coke Zero?”—people then are just assuming it’s all shit. So that’s also a problem. Actually, it would be so much more productive to say: We are not in support of AI. That would actually resonate with people, because it’d be news without AI. I think that you could actually wholly market a news organization off of that.

I hate this, because I’m a big believer in the open internet, but I actually think that news organizations right now need to create siloed universes where people will build reputational trust with an organization, because it’s not AI slop. Within five years, the majority of things we see on the internet will just be AI slop. It’s already there. So why not create a website that people can actually trust, written and curated by humans?

And Reed was gesturing at that. At the idea of being this oasis of trust in a sea of slop.

Then why put out AI slop?

Let’s talk about their deal with Palantir. USA Today’s execs told me Palantir works only with “highly controlled” data and has no access to newsroom systems or reporters’ notes, and accused the union of spreading fear and falsehoods about the deal. What did you make of that? 

My general reaction was just one of disappointment that both [president of USA Today Media] Kristin Roberts and Mike Reed have been so far removed from working in a newsroom that they forgot what it was like to have an organization that’s powered by journalists. They came off as extremely defensive of the relationship with Palantir, which has actively been working for ICE and DHS [Department of Homeland Security], which is not only a major news topic right now, but also is an organization that has actively assaulted journalists in city streets in the United States. We’ve had to file three separate lawsuits on it because it’s been so bad. So it’s really disappointing that they can’t see how this is an ethical issue, that this is a safety issue, that there’s a security issue here. 

Palantir has worked with or is working with a number of media organizations, including Axel Springer and Fox News. What specifically are union members concerned about?

What are you actually doing with readers’ data here? What are you losing control over? And then they came out swinging in defense of what Palantir has access to in terms of their journalists’ data. They’ve only now offered some clarity in your interview, when they have refused to do it until this point. But there’s much that’s still unclear. 

I also wonder about how one goal of the partnership—targeting readers using “anonymized” data—impacts the relationship with readers. Of course, many media organizations target their audiences with ads.

Reporters in the group chat say they’ve heard from readers who are really concerned about this relationship, what it means about their data. So that’s been an open question. 

Instead of using Palantir, they could find a good data journalist who could look at Google Analytics and help you figure out that this actually does better here and that does better there. And this webpage is taking three minutes to load: Maybe we should fix that?

I think some of the best things that work for us—this is so basic that it sounds stupid—is literally creating decently written newsletters that bring readers in and center their concerns. Here’s this newsletter from a local reporter; here’s a human being who wrote this. And it’s not just headlines and links. It’s literally, this is what happened in your neighborhood in New York City over the last day. That’s what people are hungry for, and it’s not rocket science. You just create and curate communities where people actually want to congregate and learn.

What else have journalists been pushing for specifically when it comes to AI in the newsroom?

So there’s notification—this is what we won the Politico arbitration over. Politico didn’t notify its workers and journalists that they were rolling out new tools. One was a report builder tool, and it was supposed to be based off of the archive. And our members asked it, “Is abortion legal in the United States of America?” And it was like, “Yes, ever since Roe v. Wade.” And it just totally missed the story, broken by its own journalists, that showed that the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. So we filed arbitration for that one, and they shut down the tool—they had violated the contract, which required 60 calendar days’ notice of any new tool.

And how about compensating journalists if their work has been used in AI training and inference? 

The compensation piece has been a real challenge. There’s not been a company, a news company, that’s agreed to compensate journalists. There’s a prohibition on training off of work by a journalist if they don’t get their consent. So you need consent if you’re going to have anything trained. 

The New York Times [Company], for instance, has a deal with Amazon for AI and their content, and they have refused to provide compensation to New York Times journalists. Which is wild, because if a newspaper in Brazil picks up a story from the Times, the journalists get compensated for it.

It seems like the media companies are still trying to figure out the compensation schemes themselves. Isn’t some kind of compensation essential to the future of the business?

So many of these news companies are entering these dumb deals with AI companies, though they don’t know how much the Atlantic deal is worth versus the New York Times deal versus the McClatchy or the Gannett deal. They don’t know the cost. You’d think that they’d know how to bargain better, but they are bargaining in the dark and then accepting peanuts for something that these AI companies are just hungry for, which is original content. And that’s being stolen from all these journalists.

How do you think AI tools could be valuable for journalism?

I think that there could be some that were valuable if they were for a specific purpose. You look at The New York Times’s Manosphere Report, which basically looks at and transcribes hundreds of hours of podcasts from right-wing podcasters and then turns that into an internal email report that goes to Times journalists. That’s really helpful, because it saves you the time of having to listen to a lot of podcasts. And then it gives you a sense of, well, is there a particular trend that is happening in this particular area? Analyzing millions of records from Jeffrey Epstein being released by the government—that’s helpful. Transcribing interviews—that’s helpful. 

But it all needs to be checked. Every single one of these things has to be checked. You can’t just publish it and just say it’s the truth because it came from the machine. 

But back to Gannett. There’s another AI tool called Streamer, which essentially pulls from the archive and puts together short-form videos with AI-generated text and voiceover. The main problem, journalists say, is that it sucks. It’s not good. And there’s a 10-year-old internal tool that’s better than the AI tool.

Have you personally found a way to use AI that’s helpful, that’s reasonable?

In my union work, I have been unimpressed with its lack of accuracy. I could see ways, maybe, at some point, where it could be helpful to try and do comparisons of contracts, but I’ve just seen it fail.

Back when I was working at the L.A. Times, one of my coworkers was building a machine learning system to build a big database of recipes, because recipes are structured data. Then you can point the machine learning algorithm at the newspaper from a hundred years ago, at a PDF, and say: Figure out where the list of ingredients is, the ordered list of operations. That was a really helpful tool. And that was more than 10 years ago. 

I think organizing large sets of data is really interesting. Like the Epstein stuff. Or if you’ve got a large cache of, say, the archive of the Guild newspaper, and you want to find letters about constitutional questions. We just published our archive on our website, this printed newspaper that goes back to 1933. It’s 1,300 PDFs—huge. That’s an area where, if you’ve got a ton of documents, it’s actually helpful. Not to provide verified truths from the AI model, but to be able to say, “Well, how many times was automation mentioned in the 1930s?” And then have it directly cite, say, page 4 of this issue. And then you’d have to go back as a human and check it.

Kristin Roberts mentioned an internal chatbot at USA Today that helps reporters with FOIA [Freedom of Information Act] requests. Are there other ways that AI might be useful in newsrooms, or things that you’d like to see management do with it?

In my old job, I would scrape websites, like transit agencies and police departments. And I’d be creating a spreadsheet, so I’d have to write these scripts in Python. One thing that’s nice is you could actually speed that up a bit using AI. What would take me weeks and weeks to work on scraping is something that I could do much faster, because I’m able to use a system that has been trained on a ton of Stack Overflow pages and can say, here’s the programming language. It’s still important to know what the language that’s coming out says, so that you know it’s not just hacking the website or making things up. You’ve got to double-check it. 

And there’s definitely an argument, too, that we should just have more staff to be able to do it, because Mike Reed’s ultimate argument here is, this is going to free us up to do more things. But you’ve already cut the staff so much. You need to instead just hire staff to do the actual journalism, not try to find tools to fix a problem that you’ve created by cutting the staff so much. 

Beyond jobs, what are you hearing about AI’s impact on the process of reporting and writing itself?

Besides the jobs, I think an overarching issue is that a lot of the executives at news companies don’t actually understand what AI does, and they’re just trying to push it out. So we see that, whether it’s Axel Springer or McClatchy or Gannett, they’re all just these guys at the top who think that this is a good idea because they were with one of their millionaire friends who said this is a good thing, and they just believed them, and they don’t actually know what the systems are doing. 

I think the other thing in this moment of AI is, it actually makes it harder for journalists, because there’s so much AI slop and misinformation. And so it’s making it harder for journalists to know what’s true. 

Are there certain areas of coverage that newsrooms need to be paying more attention to now?

I think that having accountability reporting is really, really key right now, because when we lose journalists at the local level, that costs us money. When we don’t have someone who’s watching city council, watching our school boards, that means that the elected officials then can just do whatever the hell they want. So accountability is the big thing, and they’ve been shifting away from that. McClatchy has also done a major shift away from that, which has been really horrible. They laid off 30% of our represented membership in September. They got rid of a lot of accountability.

So how about, don’t lean into the very unpopular thing that people say is bad for society, and instead focus on humans that are telling stories and holding power to account. Because that’s been a working formula for thousands of years. Ever since we started grunting around as Neanderthals, we were telling stories.

Building a data center in a company town could mean less resistance.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Starbase, Texas, which hosts SpaceX’s Starship rocket program, has just posted a notice of a public hearing for a gas-fired power plant and supercomputing facility within the corporate limits of the city. The project has an initial cost of $24 billion and will apparently be owned by SpaceX. Bloomberg reports that the project could face resistance from incoming Texas governor Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned against approving new data centers until the state's legislature has enacted stronger protections against potential harms from those projects.

Until now, Elon Musk's SpaceXSI has been building out its Colossus I and Colossus II data centers near the Mississippi-Tennessee border, but those projects have faced backlash, attracting a lawsuit from area residents that aims to curb the pollutants produced by the large number of gas turbines required to power those facilities.

Now, it seems that SpaceXSI wants to build another site in Texas that would lie in a city that mostly sits on land owned by SpaceX and whose population mostly comprises its own employees. The project might face reduced local opposition compared to the company's Memphis facilities, as Starbase is essentially a company town for SpaceX. But Hinojosa's arrival in the governor's office could trump that seemingly permissible local regulatory climate.

The project would seem to be a part of SpaceX’s push to build 10 gigawatts of compute in 2027 alone, and the $24 billion budget for this new facility could make it one of the biggest and most expensive data center projects focused on a single site. The company's announcement also notes that the $24 billion outlay it foresees was only for the “initial phases of the projects” and that it could “include future expansions.” That suggests that SpaceXSI could invest in more capacity in Starbase, Texas, going forward, assuming the favorable regulatory climate the company likely hoped for in the area holds.

Beyond its new terrestrial ambitions in Starbase, SpaceX also remains hard at work on launching data centers into space. Musk has already laid out the plans for a first-generation AI1 compute satellite with a 150kW peak compute payload, and submitted a proposal to build a 1-million-satellite Orbital Data Center System to the FCC. That work could accelerate after data center measures lost big in the poll in the recent U.S. midterm elections. In a post-election post on X, Musk ventured that “data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

#10514. Microsoft is winding down its Oracle deal. It could be a sign of what’s to come

In late September, news circulated that the hyperscaler Oracle had sent a force majeure notice to the developer of its New Mexico data center campus, Project Jupiter, seeking to delay payments on the project should it fail to come on line in 2028 as planned. In response, Oracle took to X, writing that “force-majeure notices are commonplace in developments of this scale. They do not, by themselves, establish a project delay or change delivery expectations.” 

The hiccup was one in a series. According to Financial Times reporting from September, loans tied to the project had been “privately quoted at 89 to 91 cents on the dollar by syndicated banks like Santander and Jefferies,” reflecting, more broadly, Oracle’s barely-above-junk credit rating and its place as the company to watch for those who are concerned about an AI bubble bursting soon. That fact is made crystal clear by both press surrounding the subject and the strength of the market for Oracle credit-default swaps (essentially insurance against Oracle defaulting on its debt).

Things have since gotten worse for Oracle. Last week, overlooked by many amid the midterms and unfolding drama at Nvidia, the Financial Times reported that Oracle canceled an estimated $7 billion chip deal with the Chinese tech giant Tencent under pressure from the Trump administration. Two days later, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft had been winding down a 2023 deal to rent AI computing from Oracle that had originally been arranged to meet the computing demands of its Copilot AI assistant.

Microsoft reportedly walked away because Oracle’s Nvidia chips were already outdated—a growing concern for investors financing expensive AI infrastructure that risks becoming obsolete before it can pay for itself. As one fund manager put it colorfully to the Financial Times:

“It’s like financing a fax machine and then someone invented email.”

If Microsoft was in fact dissatisfied with the chips, this marks one of the more significant manifestations of the chip-lifecycle concern, which so far has seemingly lived in analysts’ forecasts. It also bears out the problem of mismatched timelines. Oracle is operating on decade-plus horizons, in one sense, with its data center development. But the pressure to meet short-term obligations with big swings and the need for labs to develop their frontier models mean that the build-out goings-on are happening in large part on very different timelines—year to year or even month to month.

Oracle predictably pushed back on X, saying demand for its AI infrastructure remains strong, even for older Nvidia chips. The company said that in its first quarter (which runs from June through August), it renewed or resold capacity using GPUs that were mostly at least four years old, securing long-term contracts at a 20% premium over previous pricing.

While it might seem that Oracle is continuously and unnecessarily sticking its neck out on social media to combatively address every single concern about its financing practices, the company’s posting habits make sense in an environment characterized by rising interest rates and reemergent concern about the AI bubble. Oracle has financed its build-out with more leverage than its peers and similarly negative cash flow. And it’s failed to quell concerns about its borrowing. Earlier this month, it burned through the entire $20 billion fundraising cap meant to last through fiscal 2030, just five days after announcing it. And it’s not only the leverage itself that has watchers concerned—or, doubly the economic consequences of the war in Iran—but also electoral politics.

Compounding Oracle’s troubles are two broader threats to the AI build-out: a growing political backlash against data centers and mounting investor anxiety over infrastructure spending.

In the midterms, voters approved 40 of 41 ballot measures aimed at restricting data center construction. In New Mexico, Governor-elect Deb Haaland pledged to impose a moratorium on new large-scale data centers, declaring during her campaign that Oracle’s Project Jupiter would “not exist” if she were governor.

Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq has fallen into a correction, interrupted only occasionally by rallies fueled by Anthropic’s forthcoming IPO and positive earnings from CoreWeave. On Tuesday, SoftBank reported a $7 billion quarterly loss, attributed in part to U.S. data center spending, sending shares of infrastructure companies like the turbine maker GE Vernova lower. On Wednesday, shares rallied again, with the press once more crediting CoreWeave and excitement around Anthropic’s IPO, which has been described as “too big to fail.”

While Oracle has done little to generate any good press, Larry Ellison has not helped. In September, an Oracle proxy filing revealed that he had pledged billions in shares as collateral for personal loans, which reporting would later reveal was to assist with the equity financing in his son’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. While Oracle and its board seem not too concerned—Ellison is the only executive permitted to pledge stock as collateral—the move’s specifics received some warranted attention. 

By pledging stock as collateral rather than selling it, as he had reportedly first intended, Ellison appeared to be attempting to keep his full stake intact while avoiding the headlines a sale would inevitably generate. This in itself isn’t bad news for Oracle, but such a high level of borrowing nonetheless raises more conventional concerns about corporate governance. By tying his personal borrowing to Oracle’s fluctuating share price, Ellison has created a scenario in which a falling stock price could prompt lenders to demand more collateral or force a sale that would push the stock even lower. Unlikely, true—Oracle has written in SEC filings that Ellison has “the financial capacity to repay his personal term loans without resorting to the pledged shares”—but it’s hardly what Oracle needs right now.
